This way of addressing the angels by way of rebuke is set beside the words said to Noah when he pleaded that his son was of his family and that Allah's promise is the truth, and was told not to ask about what he had no knowledge of, lest he be among the ignorant. The angels had likewise asked to be made deputies on the earth so that they might glorify and sanctify Allah there.

A rival statement is then criticized as one part of which nullifies another. Whoever advanced it claimed that if you are truthful works like a man saying tell me of this if you know it, while knowing that the other does not know it, so that the words would mean he is ignorant. The answer is that there is no doubt the meaning is if you are truthful in your statement or in your action, since truthfulness in Arab speech is truthfulness in a report and not in knowledge. Some exegetes did explain it as since you are truthful, but if the particle carried that sense its vowel would have to be different, because the word for since, after a verb in the future tense, becomes a ground and a cause for that verb.

phrases.translation: They replied, “Glory be to You!
phrases.ar: قَالُواْ سُبۡحَٰنَكَ
phrases.explanation:
This is a notification of the angels returning to their Lord, acknowledging that knowledge of what they did not know belongs to Him, and disavowing any claim that they, or anyone else, would know anything of themselves.

The verse is then read as a proof in favor of the Prophet against the Jews in his midst, since Allah initiated him into knowledge of the unseen into which He had initiated none of His creatures. Allah had already rejected the angels' claim to be the fitter deputies, and He here admonishes those People of the Book, reminding them of the blessings given to their fathers, to turn back to Him and to His obedience.

phrases.translation: We have no knowledge except what You have taught us. You are truly the All-Knowing, All-Wise.”
phrases.ar: لَا عِلۡمَ لَنَآ إِلَّا مَا عَلَّمۡتَنَآۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ
phrases.explanation:
The two names are then explained. All Knowing means that Allah knows without having been taught everything that has been and everything that will be, and knows the unseen, in contrast to all His creation, whose members had just said that they have no knowledge except what He taught them. The words are therefore the angels' own conclusion drawn against themselves.

As for the Wise, some said it carries the sense of the one who judges and rules, in the same way that All Knowing carries the sense of the one who knows and the Well Informed that of the one who is informed. The pattern is that these intensive forms name the one who possesses the quality completely.

phrases.translation: Allah said, “O Adam! Inform them of their names.”
phrases.ar: قَالَ يَٰٓـَٔادَمُ أَنۢبِئۡهُم بِأَسۡمَآئِهِمۡۖ
phrases.explanation:
The command to Adam is explained by what it achieved. Allah caused His angels, who had asked to be made the deputies on the earth and described themselves as obedient in contrast to others who would spread corruption and shed blood, to recognize that they were ignorant, before He informed them, of the places on which His decree descends, as they were ignorant of the names set before them, since that belonged to what He had not taught them.

They and the rest of the servants know nothing except what their Lord has taught them, and He gives particular knowledge to whomever He wills and withholds it from whomever He wills.

phrases.translation: Then when Adam did, Allah said, “Did I not tell you that I know the secrets of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?”
phrases.ar: فَلَمَّآ أَنۢبَأَهُم بِأَسۡمَآئِهِمۡ قَالَ أَلَمۡ أَقُل لَّكُمۡ إِنِّيٓ أَعۡلَمُ غَيۡبَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَأَعۡلَمُ مَا تُبۡدُونَ وَمَا كُنتُمۡ تَكۡتُمُونَ
phrases.explanation:
Inform them means inform the angels, the pronoun referring to them, while of their names means the names of those Allah set before them. The interpreters then differed about what the revealing and concealing refer to.

The saying held most fitting is that I know what you reveal means I know, alongside My knowledge of the unseen of the heavens and the earth, what you make manifest with your tongues, and what you were concealing means what you hid within yourselves, so their secrets and their open words stand equal before Allah. What they made manifest was the question reported of them above, and what they concealed was the contradiction and pride Iblis carried against Allah's command.

A second possibility, that the angels concealed a claim to be more honored than any creature Allah might make, is judged to have no proof in the Book or in a binding tradition.

An objection is answered. A report of what the angels concealed, though put as a report about all of them, can carry a meaning about Iblis alone, because the Arabs, reporting about part of a group without naming anyone, phrase it as a report about all.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam,”
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ قُلۡنَا لِلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ ٱسۡجُدُواْ لِأٓدَمَ
phrases.explanation:
The opening is joined grammatically to the clause before it, so it continues the reminder of favors addressed to the Jews in the place of the Prophet's emigration, listing what Allah did for them and for their father Adam. Singling Iblis out from among them is read as showing that he was one of them.

Whether he belonged to the angels was disputed. Some said the jinn are a branch of the angels, a tribe of them, and that his tribe was called the jinn, since the Arabs so name whoever hides himself and is not seen.

The arguments on the other side are judged to show the weakness of their authors' knowledge. It is not strange that Allah created the kinds of His angels from different kinds of creation, some from light and some from fire, and His reporting what Iblis was made from does not put him outside their number. Nor does having offspring remove him from them, since desire was built into him.

phrases.translation: so they all did—but not Iblîs,
phrases.ar: فَسَجَدُوٓاْ إِلَّآ إِبۡلِيسَ
phrases.explanation:
The name is explained as a word on a derived pattern meaning despair of good, regret and grief, and a poet's use of the same root is glossed as dejection and gloom.

A question of grammar follows. If the name is built on that pattern, why was it not fully declined and given the nunation that a regular Arabic noun takes? The answer is that full declension was dropped because of its weight, since it is a name with no equal among the names of the Arabs, and they therefore treated it like the borrowed names that are not declined. Another name is cited as parallel, one derived from an Arabic verb yet left without nunation because it was first a name among non Arabs and was then adopted, and a third name is given the same account.

phrases.translation: who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful
phrases.ar: أَبَىٰ وَٱسۡتَكۡبَرَ وَكَانَ مِنَ ٱلۡكَٰفِرِينَ
phrases.explanation:
He refused means that Iblis refused to prostrate before Adam, and he acted arrogantly means that he thought himself great and too proud to obey Allah in prostrating before him. Although this is a report about Iblis, it is read as a rebuke to his likes, to everyone too proud to submit to Allah's command.

Becoming unfaithful is then explained. Allah described Iblis in the same terms as those for whom He set him as an example in arrogance and envy, meaning that he denied Allah's favors by opposing Him in what He commanded. The same denial is charged against the Jews, who saw the Prophet and beheld Allah's proof in him, then denied his prophethood after knowing it.

phrases.translation: We cautioned, “O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise
phrases.ar: وَقُلۡنَا يَٰٓـَٔادَمُ ٱسۡكُنۡ أَنتَ وَزَوۡجُكَ ٱلۡجَنَّةَ
phrases.explanation:
The verse is read as carrying a clear indication of the order of events. Iblis was expelled from the Garden after he refused out of arrogance to prostrate before Adam, and Adam was placed in it before Iblis came down to the earth. It follows that Iblis made them slip from obedience only after he had been cursed and had shown his arrogance, since the prostration of the angels took place after the spirit was breathed into Adam, and it was at that moment that Iblis refused.

The exegetes then differed about the state in which Adam's wife was created and the time at which she was made his companion, one report placing her creation after he entered the Garden and another placing it before he dwelt there.

The word for wife is discussed on its own account. The wife of a man is named in Arabic by a form without a final letter and by a form with one, and the form with it is the more frequent in the language, while the shorter form is explained as belonging to a particular dialect.

phrases.translation: and eat as freely as you please,
phrases.ar: وَكُلَا مِنۡهَا رَغَدًا حَيۡثُ شِئۡتُمَا
phrases.explanation: The permission is then summed up. The sense is dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat of it an ample and pleasant provision wherever you wish. The word translated freely carries the idea of provision that is wide and agreeable, and the leave given is open as to place, so nothing in the Garden is held back from them. That makes the single restriction in the next clause the only limit on a permission that is otherwise complete.

phrases.translation: but do not approach this tree,
phrases.ar: وَلَا تَقۡرَبَا هَٰذِهِ ٱلشَّجَرَةَ
phrases.explanation:
The word for tree is explained first. It covers in Arabic everything that stands on a trunk, and a verse is quoted in which the plants and the trees prostrate, the second of the two terms being what stands upon a trunk.

The exegetes then differed about which tree it was. Some said it was the ear of grain, others said the grapevine, and others said the fig tree, and reports are given for each.

The position taken is that Allah informed His servants that Adam and his wife ate of the tree their Lord had forbidden them, and so committed the sin He had forbidden, after He had pointed the tree out to them by saying do not approach this tree. He gave them the indication they needed to know which tree was meant at the time. But Allah placed no indication for His servants, to whom the Quran is addressed, as to which of the trees of the Garden it was, so the identifications offered are not something the text establishes, and the obligation carried by the verse does not depend on settling the question.

phrases.translation: or else you will be wrongdoers.”
phrases.ar: فَتَكُونَا مِنَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
phrases.explanation:
Two grammatical accounts are given of the verb that follows the prohibition. On one, it is put in the jussive by the same means as a prohibition before it, as though the prohibition were repeated, and a poet's line is cited for it. On the other, the clause carries the sense of an answer to the prohibition, so the meaning is do not approach this tree, for if you approached it you would be among the wrongdoers, as one says do not revile so and so lest he revile you.

The sense given is that they would then be among those who reach past what is permitted and allowed to them.

The word for wrongdoers is then traced to its origin, which is putting a thing in a place that is not its own. Illustrations are quoted from Arabic speech. An earth is called wronged when a digger digs in it where digging does not belong, and valley beds are called wronged when rain comes outside its season and pours where it should not. The idea branches into further senses, left to be set out where they occur, but the origin of all of them is the one described.

phrases.translation: But Satan deceived them—leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in,
phrases.ar: فَأَزَلَّهُمَا ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنُ عَنۡهَا فَأَخۡرَجَهُمَا مِمَّا كَانَا فِيهِۖ
phrases.explanation:
Two readings of the first verb are noted, the one followed here and another meaning the removal of a thing from another. The first is held more correct, since Allah reported afterwards that Iblis caused them both to depart from what they were in.

Many reports are brought in about how he brought them to it, in one of which he wailed over them until they grieved, in another he whispered first to the wife and then made the tree seem beautiful to Adam, and in another he was carried into the Garden by one of its animals.

What accords with the Book of Allah is judged most in accord with the truth. Allah reported that Iblis whispered to the two of them to show them what was hidden of their private parts, that he said their Lord forbade them the tree only lest they become angels or become immortal, and that he swore he was a sincere adviser, while bringing them down by deceit.

As for how he reached the Garden after being expelled from it, what is reported from Ibn Abbas and Wahb contains nothing a person of understanding may refute.

He caused them to depart from what they were in means from the abundant sustenance and wide bounty of the Garden. The expulsion is ascribed to Satan, though Allah expelled them, because their leaving rested on an occasion he brought about.

phrases.translation: and We said, “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other.
phrases.ar: وَقُلۡنَا ٱهۡبِطُواْ بَعۡضُكُمۡ لِبَعۡضٍ عَدُوّٞۖ
phrases.explanation:
Allah's statement that follows makes clear that the one who expelled Adam is Allah, and that the ascription to Iblis stands as described.

The interpreters differed about who is intended by the plural in descend, while agreeing that Adam and his wife are among them.

A question about the enmity named is then answered. The enmity of Iblis toward Adam and his offspring is his envy and his arrogance against obeying Allah in prostrating to him. The enmity of Adam's offspring toward Iblis is the enmity of the believers toward him because of his disbelief. The war between us is held to go back to Iblis being brought into the Garden after Allah expelled him, until he made Adam slip by eating of the forbidden tree.

phrases.translation: You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay.”
phrases.ar: وَلَكُمۡ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ مُسۡتَقَرّٞ وَمَتَٰعٌ إِلَىٰ حِينٖ
phrases.explanation:
The people of interpretation differed about the residence named here, and one explanation given was that it means an abode in the graves.

The word itself is settled from the language. It means the place of settling, so wherever anyone is on the earth at this moment, that place is his dwelling place. What Allah intended is that they have on the earth a dwelling and an abode in their locations, in place of the Garden and the heaven.

The provision mentioned with it was likewise explained in two ways, some taking it as sustenance until death and others as lasting until the coming of the Hour. The word in Arabic covers everything from which enjoyment is taken, whether sustenance, household goods, adornment, pleasure or anything else. Since Allah made the life of every living thing an enjoyment for it during the days of its life, and made the earth an enjoyment for human beings during the days of their life, by dwelling on it, by being nourished from the food and fruit He brings out of it, and by the pleasures He created in it, the enjoyment runs to the term appointed for each life, which is what both explanations describe.

phrases.translation: Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord,
phrases.ar: فَتَلَقَّىٰٓ ءَادَمُ مِن رَّبِّهِۦ كَلِمَٰتٖ فَتَابَ
phrases.explanation:
The verb translated as inspired is explained as taking the words up and accepting them, and its root is traced to a pattern derived from meeting, as when one man goes out to meet another. A variant reading is noted in which the words are made the subject that received Adam, and this is allowed to be possible in Arabic, since whatever a man receives has also received him and whatever he meets has met him, though the reading followed here is kept.

The exegetes then differed about what the words were. One report gives them as a supplication opening with the confession that there is no god but Allah. The statements transmitted are said to differ in wording while agreeing in meaning, which is that Allah extended words to Adam, that Adam received them from his Lord, accepted them and acted on them, and that through them his repentance was accepted.

What the Book of Allah itself points to is then preferred. The words Adam received are the words Allah reported him saying when he excused himself before his Lord and confessed his guilt, our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us we shall be among the losers.

phrases.translation: so He accepted his repentance. Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful
phrases.ar: عَلَيۡهِۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
phrases.explanation:
He accepted his repentance is explained with the pronoun fixed as returning to Adam, and the sense given is that Allah granted him repentance for his sin, the word itself meaning a turning back.

The two names that follow are then explained. The Ever Relenting is the one who accepts the repentance of whichever of His sinful servants turns back to Him, and who holds off from requiting him once he has turned. The Merciful means that He bestows mercy along with the repentance, and His mercy toward the sinner is the wiping out of his offense and the forgiving of the punishment his transgression had earned.

phrases.translation: We said, “Descend all of you!
phrases.ar: قُلۡنَا ٱهۡبِطُواْ مِنۡهَا جَمِيعٗاۖ
phrases.explanation:
The command to descend had already been explained earlier in the surah, and its meaning here is the same as its meaning there, so it is not gone over again.

One point is drawn out. The outward sense of the address reaches only those who were told to descend, all of them, and the people addressed are the ones named on the authority of the Companions, so the command is not read as extending beyond them on the strength of this verse alone.

phrases.translation: Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows it, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve
phrases.ar: فَإِمَّا يَأۡتِيَنَّكُم مِّنِّي هُدٗى فَمَن تَبِعَ هُدَايَ فَلَا خَوۡفٌ عَلَيۡهِمۡ وَلَا هُمۡ يَحۡزَنُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The opening particle is worked through first. The sense is if there comes to you, and the particle joined to if strengthens the utterance, which is why the doubled letter was added to the verb that follows it. Some hold the doubling became appropriate only because that particle is a negation, others that it strengthens the utterance, and others call it filler, though something disputed may not be made into a principle.

Guidance here means clarification and right direction, and whoever follows it means whoever follows the clarification Allah sent on the tongues of His messengers. No fear shall come upon them then means that they are safe amid the terrors of the Resurrection from Allah's punishment, because they obeyed Him in this life and followed His command and His path, and nor shall they grieve completes the same promise.

A further view is recorded and answered. It holds that the command to descend, though addressed to Adam and his wife, is to be understood as intended for them and their offspring, as Allah addressed the heaven and the earth together when He told them to come. The support given is that Adam after coming down to the earth was the prophet and messenger of Allah to his children. That reading is acknowledged as one the verse could bear, but is judged farther from the correct meaning than what stays closer to the outward sense of the recitation.

phrases.translation: But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire. They will be there forever.”
phrases.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ وَكَذَّبُواْ بِـَٔايَٰتِنَآ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ أَصۡحَٰبُ ٱلنَّارِۖ هُمۡ فِيهَا خَٰلِدُونَ
phrases.explanation:
Those who disbelieve and deny the signs are explained as those who rejected Allah's signs and accused His messengers of lying. The signs are His proofs and His indications of His oneness and His sovereignty, together with what the messengers brought as marks and testimonies of that and as proof of their own truthfulness in what they reported from Him.

The outcome named for them is that they are the companions of the Fire and will remain in it, which is the counterpart of the safety from fear and grief promised in the verse before to those who follow the guidance.

phrases.translation: O children of Israel!
phrases.ar: يَٰبَنِيٓ إِسۡرَٰٓءِيلَ
phrases.explanation:
The children of Israel are the children of Yaqub, the son of Ishaq, the son of Ibrahim. Yaqub was called Israel, which is explained as the servant of Allah and His chosen one among His creatures, the second element of the name being a name of Allah.

The address is then placed. It is directed to the scholars of the Jews from among the children of Israel who were present in the region to which the Messenger of Allah had emigrated, and their lineage is traced to Yaqub in the way that lineage is traced elsewhere in the Quran.

phrases.translation: Remember My favours upon you.
phrases.ar: ٱذۡكُرُواْ نِعۡمَتِيَ ٱلَّتِيٓ أَنۡعَمۡتُ عَلَيۡكُمۡ
phrases.explanation:
The favor recalled is then listed. Allah chose the messengers from among them, sent down the books on them, and saved them from the trial and affliction they were under with Pharaoh and his people, along with the provision that followed their rescue.

The reminder given here through Muhammad is set beside the reminder Musa gave their forefathers in his own time, about which Allah reported that he spoke to them, so the command to remember is of a piece with the earlier one and repeats it to a later generation.

phrases.translation: Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine,
phrases.ar: وَأَوۡفُواْ بِعَهۡدِيٓ أُوفِ بِعَهۡدِكُمۡ
phrases.explanation:
The meaning of the covenant was already set out earlier, with the disagreement over it and the judgment preferred, so it is not repeated. Here it is Allah's covenant with them, and the second half states His side of it.

His covenant with them is explained as the promise that if they did what was asked He would admit them to the Garden. The verse in which Allah took the covenant of the children of Israel and raised up twelve leaders from among them is quoted as the parallel, since it sets out the same exchange in full, with the conditions named and the reward promised.

phrases.translation: and stand in awe of Me ˹alone˺
phrases.ar: وَإِيَّٰيَ فَٱرۡهَبُونِ
phrases.explanation: Fear Me alone is explained as a command to fear Allah by Himself and to guard against His punishment. The people addressed are named as those among the children of Israel who neglect His covenant and deny His messenger, the one Allah took their oath about in the books He sent down to His prophets, that they should believe in him and follow him. The fear commanded is therefore directed at a specific refusal they are already committed to.

phrases.translation: Believe in My revelations which confirm your Scriptures.
phrases.ar: وَءَامِنُواْ بِمَآ أَنزَلۡتُ مُصَدِّقٗا لِّمَا مَعَكُمۡ
phrases.explanation:
Believe is explained as affirming something to be true, and what is to be affirmed is the revelation sent down to Muhammad. The word confirming is then given its grammatical place. It describes the state of what was sent down, referring back to the pronoun understood inside the verb, so the sense is that the new revelation confirms the scripture the addressed people already hold.

Two readings of the command that follows are set aside. One took be not the first to deny it as meaning denial of their own Book, on the ground that denying Muhammad is denying a Book that already carries his description. Another is reported from Abu al-Aliya. Both are judged to lie far from the apparent sense to which the recitation points, because the verse begins by commanding belief in what Allah sent down, and the denial spoken of is denial of that.

phrases.translation: Do not be the first to deny them or trade them for a fleeting gain.
phrases.ar: وَلَا تَكُونُوٓاْ أَوَّلَ كَافِرِۭ بِهِۦۖ وَلَا تَشۡتَرُواْ بِـَٔايَٰتِي ثَمَنٗا قَلِيلٗا وَإِيَّٰيَ
phrases.explanation:
A question of grammar is raised and answered. How can the word for disbeliever be singular when the command is addressed to a multitude? The answer is that the singular follows the sense of the word for whoever, with an explicit noun built from the verb put in its place, and that elsewhere the same idea is put in the plural. Both shapes are sound in Arabic.

The meaning is then given as an address to the community of the scholars of the People of the Book. Acknowledge as true what I sent down to My messenger of the Quran, which confirms your Book and what you already hold, and do not be the first to reject it after knowing it.

Trading the signs for a small price is explained last. The people of explanation differed about it, and the reading given is do not sell the knowledge I gave you through My Book and My signs for a contemptible price and a paltry worldly gain. Their selling of it is their holding back from making clear what they were required to make clear, in exchange for what they are paid.

phrases.translation: And be mindful of Me
phrases.ar: فَٱتَّقُونِ
phrases.explanation: Fear Me alone is explained by naming what the fear concerns. Fear Me in selling My signs for a contemptible price, in buying the paltry goods of this world with them, in disbelieving in what I sent down to My messenger and in denying him. A note on the language of satiety follows, with the saying that the food of one suffices for two and the food of two for four, since the gain they took is the kind that fills a person and leaves him base.

phrases.translation: Do not mix truth with falsehood
phrases.ar: وَلَا تَلۡبِسُواْ ٱلۡحَقَّ بِٱلۡبَٰطِلِ
phrases.explanation:
Mixing is explained from its root. The verb means to intermingle, and one says I mixed this matter up for him when one obscures a thing for someone by mingling it with something else. A second verb from the same letters is distinguished from it, the one meaning the wearing of clothes, so the two are not confused.

The mixing named in the verse is then described. Among those addressed were hypocrites who displayed affirmation of Muhammad outwardly while concealing disbelief in him inwardly, and the majority of them said that he was a prophet truly sent, but sent to the Arabs alone and not to them. That is the mixing of truth with falsehood, since they joined a true acknowledgment to a false restriction of it.

Two possibilities that the verse can bear are set out, the first reported from Ibn Abbas and the second from Abu al-Aliya and Mujahid. A point of grammar accompanies them, concerning a verb put in the accusative because it follows the same construction as the one for concealing, the sense being a single connected prohibition rather than two unrelated ones.

phrases.translation: or hide the truth knowingly
phrases.ar: وَتَكۡتُمُواْ ٱلۡحَقَّ وَأَنتُمۡ تَعۡلَمُونَ
phrases.explanation: Two interpretations of concealing the truth are noted. On the first, Allah forbade them to hide the truth just as He forbade them to mix it with falsehood, so the two prohibitions stand side by side. On the second, they form one connected act, the hiding being how the mixing is carried out. What makes the hiding culpable is the closing phrase, since they did it knowing that what they suppressed was the truth.

phrases.translation: Establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and bow down with those who bow down
phrases.ar: وَأَقِيمُواْ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتُواْ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَٱرۡكَعُواْ مَعَ ٱلرَّٰكِعِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The command is placed first. It is reported that the scribes of the Jews and their hypocrites used to tell people to establish the prayer and to give the alms tax while not doing either themselves, and this verse is read as a command to those same people to perform what they had been ordering others to perform.

Establishing the prayer is not gone over again, since its meaning was already set out earlier in the work and repeating it was avoided. The alms tax is then explained from its name. It is called by a word meaning growth and purity even though it is wealth separated from wealth, because Allah makes what is separated out bear fruit and increase, so the name belongs to it by virtue of what Allah does through it rather than by virtue of the amount.

The closing command to bow with those who bow is read as a command to join those who pray rather than to stand apart from them. It is addressed to the scribes and hypocrites named at the start, and it completes the sequence by requiring them to do in company with the believers what they had been telling other people to do.

phrases.translation: Do you preach righteousness and fail to practice it yourselves, although you read the Scripture?
phrases.ar: أَتَأۡمُرُونَ ٱلنَّاسَ بِٱلۡبِرِّ وَتَنسَوۡنَ أَنفُسَكُمۡ وَأَنتُمۡ تَتۡلُونَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَۚ أَفَلَا
phrases.explanation:
The exegetes differed about the righteousness these people were urging on others. The statements recorded are judged to be close together in meaning, so the difference in wording does not divide the sense.

The explanation whose correctness is shown by the outward wording of the recitation is then given. It runs, do you command people to obey Allah and leave yourselves disobedient, while you recite the Book. The rebuke lies in the joining of the two. The people addressed read a scripture that carries the description of the messenger and the command to follow him, and they told others to do what that scripture requires while not doing it themselves.

The form of the sentence is a question, but it is not asked in order to be answered. It is put to them as a reproach, so that the ugliness of what they were doing is stated in the shape of something they have to admit. The scribes are therefore charged with two faults at once, urging obedience they withheld and knowing the Book they were not following.

phrases.translation: Do you not understand
phrases.ar: تَعۡقِلُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The closing question is explained as do you not then understand and grasp the ugliness of what you are doing. It is not a doubt about whether they have minds but a way of saying that their conduct is one no one who understood it would keep up.

This closing is then used as confirmation of the reading given before it, namely that the scribes of the Jews among the children of Israel ordered others to follow what they themselves were not following, since a reproach about failing to understand fits a people who knew better and acted otherwise.

phrases.translation: And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is a burden except for the humble—
phrases.ar: وَٱسۡتَعِينُواْ بِٱلصَّبۡرِ وَٱلصَّلَوٰةِۚ وَإِنَّهَا لَكَبِيرَةٌ إِلَّا عَلَى ٱلۡخَٰشِعِينَ
phrases.explanation:
Patience is explained first as patience in fulfilling the covenant they had concluded with Allah and in keeping His obedience. It was also said that the word here means fasting, fasting being one of the senses the word carries in Arabic, so the two explanations are not opposed.

A question is then raised about the second half of the command. If seeking help through patience is understood as holding to the covenant and to obedience, what is the meaning of seeking help through prayer? The answer given is that prayer is the means by which the servant asks for what he cannot carry by himself, so the two are joined because one is endurance and the other is a request for the strength to endure.

The verse is then placed. Allah commanded those whose case He had described, the scholars of the children of Israel, to take their refuge in fulfilling His covenant through patience and through prayer, so the command is directed at people who already knew what the covenant required of them.

The closing clause is explained last. It is heavy means that prayer, or the covenant it serves, weighs on the person who carries it, and the weight is lifted only for the humble, who are the people described in the verse that follows. The exception is therefore not about strength of body but about a disposition, since what makes the burden light is the fear of standing before Allah that the next verse describes.

phrases.translation: those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and to Him they will return
phrases.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ يَظُنُّونَ أَنَّهُم مُّلَٰقُواْ رَبِّهِمۡ وَأَنَّهُمۡ إِلَيۡهِ رَٰجِعُونَ
phrases.explanation:
A difficulty is raised about the first word. How can Allah describe as humble in obedience people of whom He reports that they suppose, when supposing is commonly understood as less than knowing? The answer is that the word in Arabic is used for certainty as well as for doubt, and that this is a regular feature of the language rather than a loose usage. Words of the same kind are cited, one that means both darkness and light, and another that means both the one who gives help and the one who calls for it, so a single form carries two opposite senses.

Witnesses are then brought from Arabic speech and from the Quran. A speaker says be certain that two thousand armed men are coming to you, using the word for supposing where certainty is meant, and a poet is quoted to the same effect. From the Quran, the verse in which the criminals see the Fire and suppose that they are about to fall into it is cited, where what they have is not doubt but the certainty of someone looking at what is in front of him.

The word for supposing in this verse is therefore read as certainty. What the humble are certain of is stated in the two clauses that follow, and each is explained on its own. That they will meet their Lord means that they will stand before Him and be brought to account, which is the meeting the Quran speaks of for the day of judgment. That to Him they return means that their going back is to Him and to no other, so the return is not to a place but to a person who judges.

The two clauses together are what makes the burden of the previous verse light. A person who is certain that he will meet his Lord and that his return is to Him carries patience and prayer differently from someone who treats this life as the whole of things. The description of the humble is therefore completed by naming the knowledge they hold, and the whole passage from the command to seek help through patience ends by explaining who is able to do it.

phrases.translation: O Children of Israel! Remember ˹all˺ the favours I granted you
phrases.ar: يَٰبَنِيٓ إِسۡرَٰٓءِيلَ ٱذۡكُرُواْ نِعۡمَتِيَ ٱلَّتِيٓ أَنۡعَمۡتُ عَلَيۡكُمۡ
phrases.explanation: The command to remember the favor is explained here in the same way as in the earlier verse where the same words occur, so the explanation is not repeated. What is recalled is the favor Allah bestowed on them, and the address runs to the descendants of those on whom it was bestowed.

phrases.translation: and how I honoured you above the others
phrases.ar: وَأَنِّي فَضَّلۡتُكُمۡ عَلَى ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The preference named is also part of what Allah brings to their remembrance of His blessings on them. It is then limited in scope. The explanation preferred is that they were preferred above the worlds of their own time, that is, above the peoples who lived alongside them, rather than above every people until the end of the world.

The proof offered for that limitation is a narration from the Prophet which makes clear that the children of Israel were not preferred above the community of Muhammad. Since a later community is held to be greater, the preference claimed in the verse cannot be an absolute one, and the reading that confines it to the people of that time is the one that fits both the verse and the narration.

phrases.translation: Guard yourselves against the Day
phrases.ar: وَٱتَّقُواْ يَوۡمٗا لَّا
phrases.explanation:
The command to guard against a day is a warning from Allah to the people addressed, and the day is described by what will not happen in it rather than by what will.

A point of grammar is settled along the way. Something referring back to the day is left unspoken in the clause that follows, and it is omitted because what comes after is a sufficient indication of it, so the listener supplies it without being told. Some grammarians held that the omitted element could be nothing other than that pronoun, while others allowed a wider range, and both positions are reported.

phrases.translation: on which no soul will be of help to another.
phrases.ar: تَجۡزِي نَفۡسٌ عَن نَّفۡسٖ شَيۡـٔٗا
phrases.explanation:
The verb translated as be of help is traced to its root, which in Arabic means satisfaction and recompense. One says I satisfied him his loan and his debt, using the same verb. The scholars of the language then differed about two related forms, some holding that one means I satisfied on your behalf and the other I did sufficiently, and others holding that both carry a single meaning.

The question is put, what does it mean that no soul can satisfy for another soul or bring it any benefit, and the answer is that it cannot discharge what the other owes. A claim by some grammarians of Basra that the sense is that one soul cannot take the place of another is rejected, on the ground that if that had been the meaning the wording would have been different from what was used.

phrases.translation: No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given
phrases.ar: وَلَا يُقۡبَلُ مِنۡهَا شَفَٰعَةٞ وَلَا يُؤۡخَذُ مِنۡهَا عَدۡلٞ وَلَا هُمۡ يُنصَرُونَ
phrases.explanation:
Intercession is explained from its root, a verbal noun taken from saying that so and so interceded for me with so and so. The verse is then read as a whole. Guard yourselves against a day on which no soul can discharge for another soul a right owed to Allah or owed to another person, on which no intercession is accepted from it, on which no ransom is taken from it, and on which no help is given to it.

The reason those four things are named is given. Allah addressed the people this verse concerns in this way because they were Jews who held that their righteous forefathers would intercede for them with Allah and so save them from His punishment. The verse deprives them of that hope, since it states plainly that on the day in question no intercession from a soul is accepted and no ransom taken, however the person claiming it may be related to the righteous.

A distinction is then drawn so that the verse is not read as a denial of intercession altogether. It is made clear that Allah may remit for His believing servants through the intercession of the Prophet on their behalf. The denial here concerns the day as it faces those who die rejecting what Allah sent, and it removes the specific claim these people were relying on, not the intercession Allah Himself permits for believers.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh,
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ نَجَّيۡنَٰكُم مِّنۡ ءَالِ فِرۡعَوۡنَ يَسُومُونَكُمۡ
phrases.explanation:
The word for people is explained first. It is used properly with names that are well known, as in the house of the Prophet or the kin of a named man, so the people of Pharaoh are those attached to him and following him rather than his family in the narrow sense.

Pharaoh himself is then described. It is said that the name was a title given to the kings of the Amalekites in Egypt, in the same way that some Roman rulers were called by one title and some Persian rulers by another. The particular Pharaoh of Moses is reported to have been named, and the report is given.

A question follows about the address. How is it right to say We delivered you when the people being spoken to never met Pharaoh and were not present at any of it? The answer is that the favor bestowed on the forefathers is spoken of as bestowed on the descendants, because what befell the ancestors is counted among the blessings and the trials of the people who came from them. A poet is cited as a parallel, one who spoke of a battle day he never witnessed and of a man he never met, because the day belonged to the people he was addressing.

phrases.translation: who afflicted you with dreadful torment,
phrases.ar: سُوٓءَ ٱلۡعَذَابِ يُذَبِّحُونَ أَبۡنَآءَكُمۡ
phrases.explanation:
The dreadful torment is explained as the punishment that did them evil, and some said it means the most severe punishment. The question is then asked what that punishment was, and the verse answers it in the two clauses that follow.

A point about the ascription is settled. Allah ascribes to the people of Pharaoh what was done to the children of Israel, the imposition of the dreadful torment and the slaughtering of the sons, even though the order came from Pharaoh himself. The deeds are named as theirs because they carried them out, and this is how Arabic speech attributes the acts of a people to the whole of them.

The explanation of the slaughtering of the sons and the keeping of the women alive is then given as it was reported, along with the reason the two were joined in one policy.

phrases.translation: slaughtering your sons and keeping your women. That was a severe test from your Lord
phrases.ar: وَيَسۡتَحۡيُونَ نِسَآءَكُمۡۚ وَفِي ذَٰلِكُم بَلَآءٞ مِّن رَّبِّكُمۡ عَظِيمٞ
phrases.explanation:
A dissenting explanation of keeping your women is recorded. Ibn Jurayj took it in a way that departed from what the others said, and those who hold that view are criticized for leaving the explanation given by the people of explanation among the Companions and those who followed them. The reading preferred is the one that agrees with Ibn Abbas and with the statements given earlier, which takes the phrase in its plain sense of sparing the women while killing the sons.

The trial mentioned with it is then explained in two steps. In that means in what We did for you, namely Our saving you from the state you were in, so what is named here is the deliverance and not only the suffering that went before it. The word translated as test is also explained as meaning a favor, with a witness quoted for that use, because its origin in Arabic speech is testing and trial, and it came to be used of good and of evil alike since a test can be carried out by either. That is why a deliverance can be called by the same name as the torment it ended.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea,
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ فَرَقۡنَا بِكُمُ ٱلۡبَحۡرَ
phrases.explanation:
The clause is joined grammatically to the one before it, so this is a second item in the same list of favors. We parted the sea for you is then explained as We divided the sea for you, and the manner of it is given. They were twelve tribes, so the sea was split into twelve paths, one for each tribe.

Some grammarians of Basra read the construction differently, taking the sense to be that Allah separated between them and the sea rather than divided the sea for them, and that position is reported alongside the first.

Before your very eyes is then explained. It means that they looked on at the parting of the sea and at the destruction of the people of Pharaoh, so nothing in the event was hidden from them. The purpose of recalling it is stated as well. Allah brings them to a halt at the place of His proofs against them and reminds them of His favors toward their forefathers.

phrases.translation: rescued you, and drowned Pharaoh’s people before your very eyes
phrases.ar: فَأَنجَيۡنَٰكُمۡ وَأَغۡرَقۡنَآ ءَالَ فِرۡعَوۡنَ وَأَنتُمۡ تَنظُرُونَ
phrases.explanation: A question is raised about how Allah drowned the people of Pharaoh and saved the children of Israel in the same event, and the answer is given from the reports of what happened at the sea. The two acts are named together because they were one happening seen from two sides, the rescue of one group and the destruction of the other, and both took place while the people addressed were watching.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We appointed forty nights for Moses, then you worshipped the calf in his absence,
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ وَٰعَدۡنَا مُوسَىٰٓ أَرۡبَعِينَ لَيۡلَةٗ ثُمَّ ٱتَّخَذۡتُمُ ٱلۡعِجۡلَ مِنۢ بَعۡدِهِۦ
phrases.explanation:
The appointment is discussed first. Two readings of the verb are recorded, both transmitted by the community and recited by the reciters, and the judgment given is that both are sound, so the verse is read either as Allah appointing a term or as Allah making an appointment with Moses. An objection is answered along the way, namely the claim that an appointment of this kind can only be between people and that Allah stands alone in promising and threatening. That claim is judged to have no validity against a recitation the community carries.

The name Moses is then explained. It is reported to be two words in Coptic meaning water and tree, the first part being the word for water and the second the word for a tree, and he was named from them because of where he was found. His lineage is given after that, tracing him through Imran back to Levi, then to Jacob who is Israel, then to Isaac and Abraham.

With the man named and the term fixed at forty nights, the verse turns to what the people did during it. They took the calf after he had gone, and that is the favor recalled here, since the appointment itself was a gift to them.

phrases.translation: acting wrongfully
phrases.ar: وَأَنتُمۡ ظَٰلِمُونَ
phrases.explanation: Wrongdoing is explained from its root sense. It is putting a thing where it does not belong, and what they did was place worship in a position other than its proper one. Worship belongs to Allah alone, and they gave it to a calf, so the closing phrase names the act as a wrong done to the order of things and not merely as a lapse.

phrases.translation: Even then We ˹still˺ forgave you so perhaps you would be grateful
phrases.ar: ثُمَّ عَفَوۡنَا عَنكُم مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ ذَٰلِكَ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَشۡكُرُونَ
phrases.explanation:
Pardon is explained first as restraint. Allah refrained from striking them with punishment immediately after what they had done, and that holding back is what the word covers here, rather than a wiping out that leaves no trace of the matter.

The closing clause is then explained. So that perhaps you would be grateful means so that you would be grateful, and the word translated as perhaps is discussed in this context, since it does not carry doubt on the part of the one who speaks. The sense of the whole is then given. Allah pardoned them after they had taken the calf as a god, so that they would be grateful to Him for the pardon, pardon being the kind of favor that calls for gratitude from the person who receives it.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We gave Moses the Scripture—the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺ that perhaps you would be ˹rightly˺ guided
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ ءَاتَيۡنَا مُوسَى ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَٱلۡفُرۡقَانَ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَهۡتَدُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The two things given to Moses are explained together. The Book is the Torah, and the Criterion is read as that which separates truth from falsehood. Two interpretations of how the two names relate are recorded, and the one judged most fitting is what came from Ibn Abbas, Abu al-Aliya and Mujahid.

A point of grammar supports that choice. The word for the Book stands in the place of the Torah as a description of it, which allows the name Torah to be left unspoken, and the Criterion is then appended to it as a second thing given. The meaning of the word for Book was already set out earlier as that which is written, so it is not gone over again here.

The reason this reading is preferred is given last, even though another is possible. What comes before it in the verse is the mention of the Book, and a description attached to something already named is the natural construction, so the guidance asked for in the closing clause follows from a scripture that also carries the means of telling things apart.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “O my people! Surely you have wronged yourselves by worshipping the calf,
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ مُوسَىٰ لِقَوۡمِهِۦ يَٰقَوۡمِ إِنَّكُمۡ ظَلَمۡتُمۡ أَنفُسَكُم بِٱتِّخَاذِكُمُ ٱلۡعِجۡلَ
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained as a reminder. Remember when Moses said to his people from among the children of Israel that they had wronged themselves, their wronging of themselves being their taking the calf as a god. The wrong is described as falling on them rather than on anyone else, which is why the sentence that follows is a way out rather than a threat.

Moses then commanded them to turn back from their sin and to repent to Allah from their apostasy, by showing repentance to Him and submitting to obedience. The command is therefore explained as a route back, and the harshness of what follows belongs to that purpose.

phrases.translation: so turn in repentance to your Creator and execute ˹the calf-worshippers among˺ yourselves. That is best for you in the sight of your Creator.” Then He accepted your repentance.
phrases.ar: فَتُوبُوٓاْ إِلَىٰ بَارِئِكُمۡ فَٱقۡتُلُوٓاْ أَنفُسَكُمۡ ذَٰلِكُمۡ خَيۡرٞ لَّكُمۡ عِندَ بَارِئِكُمۡ فَتَابَ عَلَيۡكُمۡۚ
phrases.explanation:
Turning in repentance is explained as a return to obedience to their Creator and to what pleases Him. The command to kill themselves is then reported with its outcome, that their slain reached seventy thousand according to what is transmitted from Ibn Abbas, after which Allah lifted the killing from them and accepted their repentance.

The word for Creator is examined as well. A form of it is pronounced without the glottal stop, and two accounts of why are given, one deriving it from the word for dust and the other from the act of trimming a stick. Both the dropping of that sound and its replacement are judged permissible in recitation.

The closing clause of the command is explained as telling them that their repentance carried out through the killing of themselves is better for them in the sight of their Creator, so the act is presented as a gain and not only as a penalty. The verse then reports that Allah turned in forgiveness to them, which is the acceptance that ended the matter.

phrases.translation: Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful
phrases.ar: إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
phrases.explanation: The two names are explained by returning to the meaning of repentance, already shown earlier to be a turn from what Allah detests to what pleases Him in obedience. The Ever Relenting is then described as the one who returns to His servant with what the servant loves, here the forgiving of sins and the covering of them with mercy, and the Merciful as the name that completes it. The verse ends on the acceptance rather than on the killing, so the last word is left with the two names.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We will never believe you until we see Allah with our own eyes,” so a thunderbolt struck you while you were looking on
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ قُلۡتُمۡ يَٰمُوسَىٰ لَن نُّؤۡمِنَ لَكَ حَتَّىٰ نَرَى ٱللَّهَ جَهۡرَةٗ فَأَخَذَتۡكُمُ ٱلصَّٰعِقَةُ وَأَنتُمۡ تَنظُرُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The verse is placed first. Allah made known to those He was addressing, the Jews of the children of Israel among whom the Prophet was living, what their forefathers had done, so that the reminder falls on people who claim those ancestors as their own.

The demand itself is then explained. They told Moses they would not believe him until they saw Allah openly, which is a request for a sight that removes the need for belief rather than a request for a sign that supports it. The condition is what makes the demand culpable, since it makes belief depend on something no created being is given in this life.

The punishment is discussed last. The people of interpretation differed about the nature of the thunderbolt that seized them, and several explanations are recorded one after another. What they agree on is that it came while they were looking on, which the verse states in its closing clause, so the event was witnessed by those it struck and by those who saw them struck.

phrases.translation: Then We brought you back to life after your death, so that perhaps you would be grateful
phrases.ar: ثُمَّ بَعَثۡنَٰكُم مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ مَوۡتِكُمۡ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَشۡكُرُونَ
phrases.explanation:
Raising is explained as bringing back to life, and the death named after it is the death by the thunderbolt that destroyed them. The two clauses therefore answer each other, the raising undoing exactly what the previous verse described.

The purpose clause is then explained. So that perhaps you would be grateful means that Allah did this with them so that they would be grateful to Him for the favor He bestowed on them, the favor being their return to life after they had been struck down. Gratitude is thus attached to a second gift, since the pardon mentioned earlier was the first.

A second explanation of the raising is recorded as well. Others said the meaning is that Allah sent them forth as prophets, and that view is reported alongside the first. The reading preferred is the one that fits the sequence, because the verse before it speaks of the thunderbolt striking them while they looked on, and a return to life after that is the plain sense of the words.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember when˺ We shaded you with clouds
phrases.ar: وَظَلَّلۡنَا عَلَيۡكُمُ ٱلۡغَمَامَ
phrases.explanation:
The shading is joined grammatically to the raising mentioned in the previous verse, so this is another item in the same list of favors. The word for the cloud is then explained. It is a plural formed like the word for clouds from its singular, and it names what covers the sky and wraps it.

Since the word means that which covers the sky and veils its surface from whoever looks at it, what they were shaded by is described as something spread over them rather than a single passing cloud. A poet is cited for the language, including a line in which a people are called ungrateful for a favor done to them, which is the same charge this passage of verses builds toward.

phrases.translation: and sent down to you manna and quails,
phrases.ar: وَأَنزَلۡنَا عَلَيۡكُمُ ٱلۡمَنَّ وَٱلسَّلۡوَىٰۖ
phrases.explanation:
The two foods sent down are explained one after the other. The exegetes differed about the first of them, and the explanations recorded are several. Some said it was a drink, others that it was honey, others that it was a thin bread, others that it was ginger, and others that it was what falls upon the trees and that people then eat. The verse itself names the thing without describing it, which is why the explanations differ, and what they share is that it came to them without cultivation and without labor on their part.

The second food is a bird. The name given in the verse is explained as the name of a bird resembling the quail, and a note on its form follows, that the singular and the plural share one shape in this word, as they do in the ordinary word for quail. It was also said that the singular of the word is a longer form ending in the feminine, and that report is recorded beside the first.

Both foods are described as sent down, which places them with the shading as provision given from above during the same period. That is the point of naming them together in one clause, since neither was produced by the people who ate them.

phrases.translation: ˹saying˺, “Eat from the good things We have provided for you.”
phrases.ar: كُلُواْ مِن طَيِّبَٰتِ مَا رَزَقۡنَٰكُمۡۚ
phrases.explanation:
The command to eat is explained with a point of grammar. This belongs to the kind of speech in which what is stated is enough to indicate what has been left out, and the sense here is that Allah shaded them and sent down their food while saying to them, eat of the good things with which We have provided you. The saying is understood without being spelled out.

Of the two views recorded about how this clause attaches to what precedes, the first is judged the more fitting, because the verse is describing a condition of pleasant living that Allah bestowed on them. The word for what is also noted, that it carries the sense of that which, as though it were said, eat of the good things of that which We provided you.

phrases.translation: The evildoers ˹certainly˺ did not wrong Us, but wronged themselves
phrases.ar: وَمَا ظَلَمُونَا وَلَٰكِن كَانُوٓاْ أَنفُسَهُمۡ يَظۡلِمُونَ
phrases.explanation:
Wronging is explained in the same way as before. Allah did not receive harm from what they did, and their disobedience did not diminish anything belonging to Him, so the wrong is described as falling on themselves. A note on the grammar accompanies it, this clause too belonging to the kind of speech in which what is stated indicates what has been left out.

The point is then made general. The disobedience of a disobedient person does not harm Allah and the wrongdoing of a wrongdoer does not lessen His treasures, which is why the verse can deny the wrong against Him and affirm it against them in the same breath.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We said, “Enter this city and eat freely from wherever you please;
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ قُلۡنَا ٱدۡخُلُواْ هَٰذِهِ ٱلۡقَرۡيَةَ فَكُلُواْ مِنۡهَا حَيۡثُ شِئۡتُمۡ رَغَدٗا
phrases.explanation:
The command to enter the town is explained together with the permission that follows it. Eat of it wherever you wish means a provision that is pleasant and ample, given without reckoning and without accounting, and the sense of that word was already expounded earlier in the work, so it is not repeated here.

The favor in the command lies in its openness. They are told to enter a town and eat from it wherever they wish, which removes both the question of where they may settle and the question of how much they may take. The reminder is placed at the head of the verse because the commands that follow are conditions attached to a gift already given.

phrases.translation: enter the gate with humility,
phrases.ar: وَٱدۡخُلُواْ ٱلۡبَابَ سُجَّدٗا
phrases.explanation:
Prostrating is explained as being humble and submissive, and a poet is quoted for the use of the word in that sense. The explanation given by Ibn Abbas is then set out, that the word means bowing, since the one who bows is bent over even though his posture is not a full prostration, and the two words therefore cover one act of lowering oneself.

A consequence is drawn about the next clause. On the explanation reported from Ikrima, the word for remission that follows would have to be read in the accusative, and the reasoning behind that requirement is given. A parallel is also cited from ordinary speech, the way a person says hearing and obeying to mean that he hears and obeys, which is the same construction the verse uses when it joins an act to a word said while doing it.

phrases.translation: saying, ‘Absolve us.’
phrases.ar: وَقُولُواْ حِطَّةٞ
phrases.explanation:
The word translated as absolve us is explained from its root. It is a noun on a known pattern, derived from the saying that Allah has removed your sins from you, so the word they were told to say is itself a request for the taking away of sins.

The exegetes then differed about what exactly the word amounts to. Some said something along the lines of the explanation just given, that it is a request for remission. Others said its meaning is that they were told to say there is no god but Allah, as if they directed the explanation toward saying that which removes your sins from you, since the confession of oneness is what removes them. The reports naming who held each view are given with them.

Both readings agree on the purpose of the word, which is that the people were asked to speak a sentence that acknowledges their need of forgiveness at the moment they entered the town in humility.

phrases.translation: We will forgive your sins and multiply the reward for the good-doers.”
phrases.ar: نَّغۡفِرۡ لَكُمۡ خَطَٰيَٰكُمۡۚ وَسَنَزِيدُ ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ
phrases.explanation:
Forgiving is explained as covering. Allah will cover their sins with mercy and conceal them, so that He does not disgrace them by punishing them for what they did. A witness from ordinary speech is given for the sense of covering, the way one says that a person covers another's ignorance by forbearing with him, which is concealment rather than approval.

The word for sins is then explained, with the sense that the people described by it have missed the truth and gone wrong. The closing promise is explained last. Allah will increase the doers of good, which is read as an addition beyond the forgiving already promised, so the verse moves from covering what was done badly to giving more for what is done well, and the two together are the reward attached to entering as they were told.

phrases.translation: But the wrongdoers changed the words they were commanded to say.
phrases.ar: فَبَدَّلَ ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ قَوۡلًا غَيۡرَ ٱلَّذِي قِيلَ لَهُمۡ
phrases.explanation: Exchanging is explained as altering, and the people described as wrongdoers are those who did what they were not permitted to do. The change is in the saying they were given, so the verse names it as a saying other than the one said to them, which is the word for remission they had been commanded to speak on entering the gate.

phrases.translation: So We sent down a punishment from the heavens upon them for their rebelliousness
phrases.ar: فَأَنزَلۡنَا عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُواْ رِجۡزٗا مِّنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ بِمَا كَانُواْ يَفۡسُقُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The punishment sent down is explained next. Upon those who did wrong means upon those who did what was not permitted to them, and the word for punishment is one whose meaning was already demonstrated earlier, namely punishment itself. Allah's punishment is then noted to be of various kinds, so the word does not fix a single form of it.

The reports about what was sent are weighed, and one explanation is preferred. The view reported from Ibn Zayd is judged to be the one that settles in the mind as correct, on account of a report mentioned from the Messenger of Allah, and that reasoning is given in full. The clause closes with the reason attached to the punishment, which is that they were going out of obedience, so the sending down is traced to a settled habit rather than to a single act.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said, “Strike the rock with your staff.” Then twelve springs gushed out, ˹and˺ each tribe knew its drinking place.
phrases.ar: وَإِذِ ٱسۡتَسۡقَىٰ مُوسَىٰ لِقَوۡمِهِۦ فَقُلۡنَا ٱضۡرِب بِّعَصَاكَ ٱلۡحَجَرَۖ فَٱنفَجَرَتۡ مِنۡهُ ٱثۡنَتَا عَشۡرَةَ عَيۡنٗاۖ قَدۡ عَلِمَ كُلُّ أُنَاسٖ مَّشۡرَبَهُمۡۖ كُلُواْ وَٱشۡرَبُواْ مِن رِّزۡقِ ٱللَّهِ
phrases.explanation:
Asking for water is explained as asking Allah for water for his people, that is, asking Him to provide it for them, and the people of Moses are identified as the children of Israel whose stories Allah recounts in these verses.

Two clauses are then discussed as grammar. The saying strike the rock with your staff and the gushing of the springs belong to the kind of speech in which what is stated indicates what has been left out, and the same is said of each group knew its drinking place, whose sense is that each group of them knew its place.

The reason that clause is mentioned is then given. Allah informed them of it because of their state with respect to the water He brought forth for them, since twelve springs answered to twelve groups and each was assigned its own source.

phrases.translation: ˹We then said,˺ “Eat and drink of Allah’s provisions, and do not go about spreading corruption in the land.”
phrases.ar: وَلَا تَعۡثَوۡاْ فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ مُفۡسِدِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The permission and the prohibition are joined in one address. Alongside allowing them what He allowed and bestowing on them the pleasant life He gave them, Allah addressed them with a command, so the prohibition comes attached to a favor and not on its own.

Spreading corruption is then explained as going beyond the limits and striving on the earth as corrupters. The root of the word is examined, and it is said to mean intensity of corruption, indeed the most intense form of it, with a witness quoted for the way the verb is used of someone who has gone to that extreme among people. What the verse forbids is therefore not a small fault but the worst kind of disorder, named as such right after the provision that made their life easy.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when you said, “O Moses! We cannot endure the same meal ˹every day˺.
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ قُلۡتُمۡ يَٰمُوسَىٰ لَن نَّصۡبِرَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامٖ وَٰحِدٖ
phrases.explanation: Patience is explained first, and its meaning was set out earlier as the restraining and withholding of the soul. The complaint is therefore that they could not hold themselves to a single kind of food. What they could not endure is named as one food, which is the provision that came to them in the wilderness in the same form day after day, without cultivation and without trade.

phrases.translation: So ˹just˺ call upon your Lord on our behalf, He will bring forth for us some of what the earth produces
phrases.ar: فَٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُخۡرِجۡ لَنَا مِمَّا تُنۢبِتُ ٱلۡأَرۡضُ مِنۢ بَقۡلِهَا وَقِثَّآئِهَا وَفُومِهَا وَعَدَسِهَا وَبَصَلِهَاۖ
phrases.explanation: The request is put through Moses rather than to Allah directly. They ask him to call on his Lord for them so that He brings forth for them some of what the earth grows, and what they name is the ordinary produce of settled land, herbs and cucumbers and the rest of the list that follows. The asking itself is not forbidden here, and the verse reports it without comment at this point.

phrases.translation: of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions.”
phrases.ar: قَالَ أَتَسۡتَبۡدِلُونَ ٱلَّذِي هُوَ أَدۡنَىٰ بِٱلَّذِي هُوَ خَيۡرٌۚ
phrases.explanation:
The crops named are discussed, and the disagreement falls on one word in particular. The exegetes differed about it, some saying that it means wheat and bread and others saying that it means garlic. The naming of both wheat and bread by that word belongs to the old language, and it is transmitted from speakers of that language in the form of an order, bake for us, meaning bake bread for us.

A variant reading is recorded beside it. It is mentioned that Abdullah ibn Masud read the word with a different first letter, giving the word for garlic directly. If that is correct, it belongs to the cases in which letters are interchanged between two forms of one word, and an example of such an interchange in another word is given with it.

phrases.translation: Moses scolded ˹them˺, “Do you exchange what is better for what is worse? ˹You can˺ go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for.”
phrases.ar: ٱهۡبِطُواْ مِصۡرٗا فَإِنَّ لَكُم مَّا سَأَلۡتُمۡۗ وَضُرِبَتۡ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلذِّلَّةُ وَٱلۡمَسۡكَنَةُ
phrases.explanation:
The rebuke is explained word by word. The word translated as worse is taken by some in the sense of nearer, as the comparative form of nearness, but the point is settled by the thing itself. There is no doubt that whoever exchanges the manna and the quails for herbs, cucumbers, lentils, onions and garlic has exchanged low sustenance for the high sustenance it replaced. A note on the language accompanies this, concerning a glottal stop in the word for what is near or low, reported as a dialectal variant whose omission is another variant.

Moses then asks, and the answer comes. It is explained that he called upon his Lord, that Allah answered him, and that He said to them, go down to a city. This belongs to the kind of speech in which something is left out and what is visible is enough to indicate it, since the asking and the answering are understood without being spelled out.

The city named is the largest question in the verse, and it begins with the recitation. The reciters differed about the word. Most of them read it with the full ending, which makes it a city among cities and not a particular place. Some read it without that ending and without the final letter, which makes it the Egypt of Pharaoh specifically.

The argument of those who took it as a city among cities is given. It rests on what Allah did with the land of Syria, and on His forbidding those people from entering it until they perished in the wandering of the wilderness, testing them with roaming in the land, so a command to go down to Egypt does not fit that history.

The verdict is stated plainly. In the Book of Allah there is no proof for the correctness of either explanation, and there is no report about it from the Messenger, so neither can be established on evidence. As for the recitation, however, the reading with the final letter and the full ending is the one beyond which nothing else is permissible, because the copies of the Quran held by the Muslims agree on it. The clause closes with the promise that they have what they asked for, which is the ordinary food of any settled place.

phrases.translation: They were stricken with disgrace and misery,
phrases.ar: وَبَآءُو بِغَضَبٖ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِۚ ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمۡ كَانُواْ يَكۡفُرُونَ بِـَٔايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ وَيَقۡتُلُونَ ٱلنَّبِيِّـۧنَ بِغَيۡرِ ٱلۡحَقِّۚ
phrases.explanation:
Being stricken is explained as an imposing. The word means that the humiliation and the misery were made obligatory on them, so what is described is a settled state rather than a single blow.

The humiliation is then defined. It is the lowliness which Allah commanded His believing servants to see upon those who reject Him, and the verse about fighting those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day and do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden is quoted, since it ends with their paying the tax by hand while they are humbled. That is the same word, and it fixes the humiliation as a condition imposed on a people rather than a feeling they happen to have.

The misery is explained from its root as well. It is the verbal noun of the word for the destitute, and the ordinary saying is quoted, that there is none among them poorer than a given man, which is the sense carried here.

The two together are then read as an exchange. Allah reported to them that He would give them standing in place of humiliation and ease in place of misery, so the state described in the verse is what they were left with after refusing the exchange offered to them.

phrases.translation: and they invited the displeasure of Allah for rejecting Allah’s signs and unjustly killing the prophets. This is ˹a fair reward˺ for their disobedience and violations
phrases.ar: ذَٰلِكَ بِمَا عَصَواْ وَّكَانُواْ يَعۡتَدُونَ
phrases.explanation:
Returning with wrath is explained as turning back laden with it, and the ordinary use of the verb is given. The meaning of Allah's wrath toward His servant was dealt with earlier, so it is not repeated.

The reason for the state described before it is then explained. The word translated as this refers to the imposing of the humiliation and the poverty on them, and it is imposed because they disbelieved in the signs of Allah and killed the prophets without right.

The closing clause repeats the same word a second time, which refers back to the first. The sense is that humiliation and poverty were imposed on them because they disobeyed and transgressed. Transgression is then explained as overstepping the limit Allah set for His servants toward something else.

phrases.translation: Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians—
phrases.ar: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ وَٱلَّذِينَ هَادُواْ وَٱلنَّصَٰرَىٰ وَٱلصَّٰبِـِٔينَ
phrases.explanation:
The four groups are named and explained one after the other. Those who believe are the people who hold the Messenger of Allah to be truthful in what he brought them of truth from Allah, and their faith is their affirmation of it. Those referred to by the second name are the Jews, and the verb used of them is explained as meaning that they repented, with the form of the verb given and the report that they were called by this name because of that repentance.

The Christians are explained from the same kind of root. Verses are cited to show that they were given this name because they helped one another and gave one another mutual support, and it was also said that the name comes from the question asked by Jesus, who are my helpers on the way to Allah. A third account is transmitted from Ibn Abbas by a route that is not accepted, namely that they were named after the village of Jesus, and his companions after it.

The fourth group is explained last. The word is the plural of a term meaning one who takes up a new religion alongside the religion he has, like the apostate among the people of Islam who leaves his religion, so the name covers people who have moved out of one faith without being counted in another.

A question is then raised about the sentence itself, whether it is complete with the four groups named and nothing said about them. Two answers are given. On the first, the completion of the sentence is the whole of the clause that follows, whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, and its meaning is whoever of them believes, with the words of them left out because the sense carries them. On the second, the meaning is that those who believe, and the Jews, and the Christians, and the fourth group, whoever of them believes in Allah and the Last Day has his reward with his Lord.

A longer answer rejects a reading of the first group that would make belief here mean nothing more than passing from one religion to another, as a Jew or a Christian passes into faith. The report of Salman is brought in at this point, his panic and his search for the monk, the two men of Kalb he met, the woman of Juhayna who bought him and the livestock he herded for her, and the grief that came on him, since his question about people he had lived among is what the verse answers.

What each group was required to hold is then set out. The faith of the Jews was that whoever held fast to the Torah and to the practice of Moses, until Jesus came, and did not let it go, and the same is said of the Christians in relation to what was given to them. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that Allah promised the Garden in the hereafter for righteous deeds to whoever did them among these groups, and the explanation of the verse transmitted from Mujahid and al-Suddi reads it as speaking of those who believe in this community together with the others named.

The verdict is given at the end. The first of these explanations most resembles the outward meaning of the revelation, because Allah did not restrict the reward for righteous deed joined to faith to one group and withhold it from another.

phrases.translation: whoever ˹truly˺ believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord. And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve
phrases.ar: مَنۡ ءَامَنَ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلۡيَوۡمِ ٱلۡأٓخِرِ وَعَمِلَ صَٰلِحٗا فَلَهُمۡ أَجۡرُهُمۡ عِندَ رَبِّهِمۡ وَلَا خَوۡفٌ عَلَيۡهِمۡ وَلَا هُمۡ يَحۡزَنُونَ
phrases.explanation:
Belief in Allah and the Last Day is explained as holding the resurrection after death on the Day of Resurrection to be true and acknowledging it, joined to righteous deeds. A point of grammar follows about a verb put in the dual form because of the meaning of the word for whoever, the verb agreeing with the sense of the word rather than with its shape, and the same is said of the parallel clause in this verse.

The two promises are then explained. No fear upon them means that no fear will come on them concerning what they will face of the terrors of the Resurrection, and they will not grieve means that they will not grieve over what they left behind of this world, so one clause removes what is ahead of them and the other what is behind.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We took a covenant from you
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ أَخَذۡنَا مِيثَٰقَكُمۡ
phrases.explanation: The covenant is explained from its form. The word is on the pattern of an instrument noun and is derived from the word for a surety, so it names a bond that makes a thing secure. What is meant by it here is the covenant Allah told them He had taken from them, which is the same bond described in the verses around this one.

phrases.translation: and raised the mountain above you
phrases.ar: وَرَفَعۡنَا فَوۡقَكُمُ ٱلطُّورَ
phrases.explanation: The mountain is explained first as a common noun. The word means the mountain in the language of the Arabs, and a line of poetry is quoted for that use. It was then said that it is the name of a particular mountain, and it is mentioned that this is the mountain upon which Allah spoke to Moses. Others said that the word names, among mountains, specifically those that bring forth vegetation, and both accounts are recorded.

phrases.translation: ˹saying˺, “Hold firmly to that ˹Scripture˺ which We have given you
phrases.ar: خُذُواْ مَآ ءَاتَيۡنَٰكُم بِقُوَّةٖ
phrases.explanation:
The command to hold firmly is discussed by the linguists, who differed about it. Some of the grammarians of Basra took the construction in a particular way, and the correct view is then stated, that every saying which is uttered and by which the intended meaning is understood is enough, so the words that follow are read as the speech the people were given.

The two parts of the command are then explained. Take what We have given you means what We enjoined upon you in the Torah, and with strength means with exertion in fulfilling what He enjoined there and made obligatory. The explanation of the verse as a whole is therefore that they were told to take what Allah imposed on them as obligations in His Book, to accept it and to act accordingly.

phrases.translation: and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful ˹of Allah˺.”
phrases.ar: وَٱذۡكُرُواْ مَا فِيهِ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَتَّقُونَ
phrases.explanation: Remembering what is in it is explained as remembering what the Book given to them contains, that is, its promise and its stern threat, its encouragement and its warning. The purpose clause follows from that, since a person who keeps those two in mind is the one who guards himself, and the guarding asked for is the fruit of the remembering rather than a separate act.

phrases.translation: Yet you turned away afterwards.
phrases.ar: ثُمَّ تَوَلَّيۡتُم مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ
phrases.explanation:
Turning away is explained as turning aside thereafter, and the form of the verb is discussed as being in substance a form built from turning. Examples of this way of speaking in Arabic are said to be more numerous than can be counted, and by it Allah means that they abandoned what they had accepted.

A witness is quoted to show how the same idiom works elsewhere. A speaker says that chains have encompassed the necks, and what is meant by it is a restraint that keeps people from what they used to do in the time of ignorance, which is the same use of a physical image for a change of conduct that the verse makes when it says they turned away after the covenant was taken and the mountain was raised over them.

phrases.translation: Had it not been for Allah’s grace and mercy upon you,
phrases.ar: ذَٰلِكَۖ فَلَوۡلَا فَضۡلُ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡكُمۡ وَرَحۡمَتُهُۥ
phrases.explanation:
