phrases.ar: أَوَكُلَّمَا عَٰهَدُواْ عَهۡدٗا نَّبَذَهُۥ فَرِيقٞ مِّنۡهُمۚ بَلۡ أَكۡثَرُهُمۡ لَا يُؤۡمِنُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The question at the head of the verse is discussed first. It is noted that what was explained earlier still applies, namely that it is not permissible for a particle to occur in the Book of Allah without a meaning, so the word translated as every time is read as carrying its own sense and not as filler.

The covenant is then explained. It is the solemn pledge which the children of Israel gave to their Lord, and the verse describes what a party of them does with it whenever it is made. Casting it aside is explained from the verb, and the pronoun attached to it is identified as referring to the covenant, so the sense is that whenever they make a covenant, a party of them throws it away behind them.

The closing words are then explained. Nay, most of them do not believe, and the sense given is that the casting aside is not the fault of a few among them but of most, which is why the verse ends by naming the majority rather than the party that broke the pledge.

phrases.translation: Now, when a messenger from Allah has come to them—confirming their own Scriptures—some of the People of the Book cast the Book of Allah behind their backs as if they did not know
phrases.ar: وَلَمَّا جَآءَهُمۡ رَسُولٞ مِّنۡ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ مُصَدِّقٞ لِّمَا مَعَهُمۡ نَبَذَ فَرِيقٞ مِّنَ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُواْ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ كِتَٰبَ ٱللَّهِ وَرَآءَ ظُهُورِهِمۡ كَأَنَّهُمۡ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The verse is explained as describing a particular group. By the words when there came to them, what is meant is the scribes of the Jews, so the people who received the messenger are named rather than left general.

The messenger and what he brought are then described. A messenger from Allah came to them confirming what was with them, and the explanation of that clause is given at length, since the confirming is what makes their response inexcusable, the new message agreeing with the book they already held.

The response is explained from the image used for it. Casting the Book of Allah behind their backs is a figurative expression, and its sense is that they put it behind them as a person puts away a thing he does not want to look at, so the picture is one of deliberate turning away.

The closing words are then explained. As though they did not know means that it was as if these people who threw the Book away had no knowledge of it at all, and the comparison is drawn because their conduct is that of someone ignorant.

phrases.translation: They ˹instead˺ followed the magic promoted by the devils during the reign of Solomon.
phrases.ar: وَٱتَّبَعُواْ مَا تَتۡلُواْ ٱلشَّيَٰطِينُ عَلَىٰ مُلۡكِ سُلَيۡمَٰنَۖ
phrases.explanation:
The people described as following are identified, and the sense given is that they followed what the devils recited, that is, what the devils composed and spread during the reign of Solomon. Two views are then recorded about who is meant by the followers. Some said that Allah meant the Jews who lived in the region to which the Messenger of Allah had emigrated, so the verse speaks of people who were alive when it came down. Others said that He meant the Jews who lived in the time of Solomon, so the verse speaks of an earlier generation. The reports naming who held each view are given.

The thing followed is then described as reciting, which is the word used of reading something aloud and repeating it, so what the devils did is presented as teaching and spreading rather than as a single act, and what they spread during that reign is the magic the rest of the verse describes.

The reign of Solomon is named as the period in which this spreading took place, and the verse goes on at once to clear him of what was attached to that period, since the next clause denies that he disbelieved. The naming of the reign is therefore not an accusation against the king but a way of fixing when the magic was circulated among them.

phrases.translation: Never did Solomon disbelieve, rather the devils disbelieved.
phrases.ar: وَمَا كَفَرَ سُلَيۡمَٰنُ وَلَٰكِنَّ ٱلشَّيَٰطِينَ كَفَرُواْ يُعَلِّمُونَ ٱلنَّاسَ ٱلسِّحۡرَ
phrases.explanation:
The denial concerning Solomon is explained first, and a question is raised about the construction of the sentence, with the manner of its precedence explained at length. Others said that the word translated as never carries the meaning of that which, and is a conjunction on what precedes it, and the reports naming who said so are given.

The clause about teaching people magic is then joined to the devils, so the teaching is described as theirs and not his. A further question is raised about whether the two angels named later are a closer specification of the people who were taught, and the answer is given at length, since the wording allows more than one way of attaching the names.

phrases.translation: They taught magic to the people, along with what had been revealed to the two angels, Hârût and Mârût, in Babylon. The two angels never taught anyone without saying, “We are only a test ˹for you˺, so do not abandon ˹your˺ faith.” Yet people learned ˹magic˺ that caused a rift ˹even˺ between husband and wife; although their magic could not harm anyone except by Allah’s Will. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them—although they already knew that whoever buys into magic would have no share in the Hereafter. Miserable indeed was the price for which they sold their souls, if only they knew
phrases.ar: وَمَآ أُنزِلَ عَلَى ٱلۡمَلَكَيۡنِ بِبَابِلَ هَٰرُوتَ وَمَٰرُوتَۚ وَمَا يُعَلِّمَانِ مِنۡ أَحَدٍ حَتَّىٰ يَقُولَآ إِنَّمَا نَحۡنُ فِتۡنَةٞ فَلَا تَكۡفُرۡۖ فَيَتَعَلَّمُونَ مِنۡهُمَا مَا يُفَرِّقُونَ بِهِۦ بَيۡنَ ٱلۡمَرۡءِ وَزَوۡجِهِۦۚ وَمَا هُم بِضَآرِّينَ بِهِۦ مِنۡ أَحَدٍ إِلَّا بِإِذۡنِ ٱللَّهِۚ وَيَتَعَلَّمُونَ مَا يَضُرُّهُمۡ وَلَا يَنفَعُهُمۡۚ وَلَقَدۡ عَلِمُواْ لَمَنِ ٱشۡتَرَىٰهُ مَا لَهُۥ فِي ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ مِنۡ خَلَٰقٖۚ وَلَبِئۡسَ مَا شَرَوۡاْ بِهِۦٓ أَنفُسَهُمۡۚ لَوۡ كَانُواْ يَعۡلَمُونَ
phrases.explanation:
What was sent down to the two angels in Babylon is discussed first in its wording. The people of knowledge differed concerning the particle used here, some taking it as a negative and others as a relative, and it is noted that it is permissible to read it with either sense, each giving the clause a different shape.

The two angels are then named, and what they did is described. They taught no one without first saying that they are a trial, so do not disbelieve, which means that the person who came to learn was warned before being taught, and the learning was left to his own choice after the warning.

What people learned from them is then described as something that brings about separation between a man and his wife, and the verse states that their magic harms no one except by the permission of Allah, so the effect is placed under His will and not under the power of the magic itself.

The loss that follows is stated in two parts. They learned what harms them and does not benefit them, and they already knew that whoever buys magic has no share in the hereafter. The verse ends by calling what they sold their souls for a wretched price, and adds that they would have seen this had they known.

phrases.translation: If only they were faithful and mindful ˹of Allah˺, there would have been a better reward from Allah, if only they knew
phrases.ar: وَلَوۡ أَنَّهُمۡ ءَامَنُواْ وَٱتَّقَوۡاْ لَمَثُوبَةٞ مِّنۡ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ خَيۡرٞۚ لَّوۡ كَانُواْ يَعۡلَمُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The wish expressed at the start of the verse is explained first. By the words if only they had believed and been God fearing, Allah means that if those who learned from the two angels the thing by which they brought about separation between a man and his wife had believed, that is, had held Allah and His Messenger to be true together with what He brought, and had feared Him, then what follows would have been theirs instead. The people spoken of are therefore the same people described in the verse before it, and the belief asked of them is stated in full rather than left general.

The reward named is then explained from its root. The word used here is a verbal noun in Arabic from the saying of a person who says that he rewarded someone with a reward, and its origin is a verb meaning that a thing returned to you. One then says that he caused it to return to you, so the reward is named from returning, which is why the same root is used for what a person comes back to at the end of an action. The explanation of the verse is that a reward from Allah would have been better for them than what they took, and the word itself carries the sense of something given back in return.

The construction of the sentence is then discussed by the grammarians. Some of the grammarians of Basra claimed that this sentence belongs to the kind in which the indication lying in the wording is enough, so that the second clause, which answers the condition, can be left unspoken because the listener supplies it. On that reading the answer to if only is understood and not stated.

Others among the grammarians of Basra rejected that claim. They held that the response to the words if only they had believed and been God fearing is the word for reward itself, and that the particle for if was answered by it even though Allah reported the matter with the completed form of the verb, and the reason for that is given, since the completed form is used here of something certain enough to be spoken of as already done.

The two positions are recorded side by side, and the difference between them concerns the grammar of the answer rather than the sense of the verse, which on either reading is that belief and fear of Allah would have brought them something better than what they chose. The verse closes by saying that they would have known this had they known anything at all, which puts the loss back on their own knowledge.

phrases.translation: O believers!
phrases.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ
phrases.explanation: The verse opens by addressing the believers directly, and the explanation of the saying is given together with the command that follows it. What is forbidden is a single word, and the people forbidden it are those who believe, so the prohibition concerns the language they use with the Prophet rather than anything in their belief.

phrases.translation: Do not say, “Râ’ina.” [Herd us!] But say, “Unẓurna,” [Tend to us!] and listen ˹attentively˺. And the disbelievers will suffer a painful punishment
phrases.ar: لَا تَقُولُواْ رَٰعِنَا وَقُولُواْ ٱنظُرۡنَا وَٱسۡمَعُواْۗ وَلِلۡكَٰفِرِينَ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٞ
phrases.explanation:
The word itself is discussed first. The exegetes differed concerning the explanation of the prohibition, and the explanations recorded are several. Some took the word in one sense, and others said that its meaning is a request that the person addressed direct his hearing toward the speaker, that is, listen to us and give us your attention. The verb behind it is explained as inclining the hearing toward someone and freeing it for him, so on this reading the word is not a bad word at all but an ordinary request for attention.

The reason for forbidding it is then discussed, and the exegetes differed about that as well. Some gave one reason. Others said that it was a word the helpers in Medina used in the time of ignorance, and that Allah forbade them to go on using it after Islam. Others again said that it was the saying of a particular Jew, named in the report, who used the word as a means of insulting the Prophet while keeping the appearance of a respectful form of address.

The point of language behind all of these accounts is then set out. Arabic contains pairs of words used with one and the same meaning, where one of the two forms carries a good sense and the other carries a sense that people avoid, and an example of such a pair is given from the word for a grape, with the Prophet's own guidance about which of the two forms to use. The same is said of the word used here, which sounds like a request for attention and also sounds like a word of contempt to anyone listening for it.

The reason for the prohibition is then placed in a wider setting. Allah had commanded the believers to honor and revere His Prophet, and this command is explained at length, since the honor owed to him is what rules out a word that could be turned into an insult. The verse therefore closes the matter by giving the believers another word to use, one that carries the same request without the risk attached to the first, and by telling them to listen, which is the thing the word was meant to ask for in any case.

phrases.translation: The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists
phrases.ar: مَّا يَوَدُّ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ مِنۡ أَهۡلِ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ وَلَا
phrases.explanation: The people named are the disbelievers among the People of the Book together with those who associate partners with Allah, and the verb used of them is explained as meaning that they do not love. The unwillingness described is therefore a settled dislike rather than a passing preference, since the word names a state of the heart.

phrases.translation: would not want you to receive any blessing from your Lord,
phrases.ar: ٱلۡمُشۡرِكِينَ أَن يُنَزَّلَ عَلَيۡكُم مِّنۡ خَيۡرٖ مِّن رَّبِّكُمۡۚ
phrases.explanation:
The two groups are joined in the grammar, the word for those who associate partners standing in the genitive by conjunction on what precedes it.

The explanation of the statement is then given. Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book do not love that any good should be sent down to the believers from their Lord, and the same is said of those who associate partners.

It is then noted that this verse carries a clear indication that Allah has forbidden the believers to lean on such people, since a person who does not want any good to come to you is not one whose support can be relied on.

phrases.translation: but Allah selects whoever He wills for His mercy. And Allah is the Lord of infinite bounty
phrases.ar: وَٱللَّهُ يَخۡتَصُّ بِرَحۡمَتِهِۦ مَن يَشَآءُۚ وَٱللَّهُ ذُو ٱلۡفَضۡلِ ٱلۡعَظِيمِ
phrases.explanation:
The answer to their unwillingness is given in the second half of the verse. Allah singles out with His mercy whom He wills, and the explanation of that is given at length, since the singling out is described as His own choice and not as something earned by the people it reaches.

The closing name is then explained. Allah is the possessor of tremendous bounty, and the clause is read as a statement that what He gives is not measured by what others want Him to give, so the bounty named here answers the wish named at the start of the verse.

phrases.translation: If We ever abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten,
phrases.ar: مَا نَنسَخۡ مِنۡ ءَايَةٍ أَوۡ نُنسِهَا نَأۡتِ
phrases.explanation:
The word for abrogate is explained from its origin. It comes from the copying of a writing, namely the transferring of a text from one copy into another, so the root sense is not destruction but replacement by something written in its place. The explanation of the clause is then given, and what is meant by whatever verse We abrogate is set out.

The consequence of that meaning is then drawn. When this is what the abrogating of a verse means, it makes no difference, once its ruling has been abrogated, whether the wording remains with the ruling removed or both are taken away together, since in either case the thing that governed conduct has been replaced. The discussion of this point is given at length, because it settles what kind of change the verse is speaking about.

The commentators then differed concerning the explanation of the words whatever We abrogate. Some took them one way and others another, and the reports naming who said each are recorded with them.

The second thing named in the verse is the causing of a verse to be forgotten, and it is placed beside abrogation as the other way in which a ruling ceases to be carried by the community. The answer that follows concerns both, since what is said next is that whatever happens to a verse, something takes its place.

phrases.translation: We replace it with a better or similar one. Do you not know that Allah is Most Capable of everything
phrases.ar: بِخَيۡرٖ مِّنۡهَآ أَوۡ مِثۡلِهَآۗ أَلَمۡ تَعۡلَمۡ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيۡءٖ قَدِيرٌ
phrases.explanation:
The replacement is then explained. We bring something better than it or like it, and the commentators differed concerning these words, some taking better in one sense and others in another. One explanation recorded is that Allah brings something better than what He abrogated, or something like it, and the reports of who held each view are given.

The meaning of better than it is then set out at length, since the comparison is not between two texts as texts but between what each of them requires of people, and the explanation turns on that.

The verse closes with a question that answers the objection behind it. Do you not know that Allah is capable of everything, which is put as the reason why a change in what He sends down cannot be used against Him, since the power to replace one ruling with another belongs to the same power that made the first one.

phrases.translation: Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs ˹only˺ to Allah,
phrases.ar: أَلَمۡ تَعۡلَمۡ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَهُۥ مُلۡكُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۗ وَمَا لَكُم
phrases.explanation:
The kingdom named is explained first, and the sense of the clause is that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, so nothing in them is outside His disposal.

A question is then raised about the form of the address. Did the Messenger of Allah not already know that Allah is capable of all this, and why is he spoken to as though the knowledge were being given to him for the first time? The answer recorded from some is that this is simply an announcement from Allah that Muhammad already knew it.

The reading preferred is then given. Even though the sentence appears on its surface as an address directed to the Prophet, in reality it is aimed at his community, and this is widespread in the language of the Arabs and eloquent among them, that a speaker casts his words in the form of an address to one person while meaning another. So Allah cast these words as an address to the Prophet while meaning by them the people of his community, who are the ones who need to be told what the verse goes on to say.

phrases.translation: and you have no guardian or helper besides Allah
phrases.ar: مِّن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ مِن وَلِيّٖ وَلَا نَصِيرٍ
phrases.explanation:
The two things denied are explained from their forms. The word for helper is a noun on a known pattern, derived from the saying of a person who says, I helped you, so I am your helper, and the two forms built from it are given.

The words besides Allah are then explained as meaning other than Allah and after Allah, so the phrase excludes every other source of protection and support at once. Guardian and helper are named together because the first covers the one who takes charge of a person's affairs and the second the one who comes to his aid, and neither is to be found for them apart from Him.

phrases.translation: Or do you ˹believers˺ intend to ask of your Messenger as Moses was asked before?
phrases.ar: أَمۡ تُرِيدُونَ أَن تَسۡـَٔلُواْ رَسُولَكُمۡ كَمَا سُئِلَ مُوسَىٰ مِن قَبۡلُۗ
phrases.explanation:
The verse is discussed first in its occasion. The people of interpretation differed concerning the reason it was revealed, and several accounts are recorded, each naming a different thing that some people asked of the Prophet. The reports are given with the names of those who transmitted them, so the question in the verse is read against a particular asking rather than as a general warning.

The particle at the head of the verse is then examined. The grammarians differed concerning the meaning of the word translated as or, since it can introduce a second alternative or can turn the sentence back on what came before, and each reading gives the question a slightly different place in the argument. The explanation preferred is given with the reasoning for it.

The comparison drawn in the verse is then explained. Asking the Messenger as Moses was asked before means asking in the way that people asked of Moses, which the earlier verses in this chapter have already described, so the warning is that the same kind of asking produced the same kind of trouble for the people who made it.

phrases.translation: But whoever trades belief for disbelief has truly strayed from the Right Way
phrases.ar: وَمَن يَتَبَدَّلِ ٱلۡكُفۡرَ بِٱلۡإِيمَٰنِ فَقَدۡ ضَلَّ سَوَآءَ ٱلسَّبِيلِ
phrases.explanation:
Exchanging is then explained. By the words whoever exchanges unbelief for faith, Allah means whoever puts one in the place of the other, so the verb carries the sense of a trade in which a thing is handed over and something else taken in return.

A second explanation of the two words is recorded beside it. It has been said that the word for unbelief in this place is used in the sense of hardship and the word for faith in the sense of ease, and the reports naming who said that are given. On that reading the exchange described is of one condition for another rather than of belief for its opposite, and both readings are left standing.

The consequence is then explained. Such a person has strayed from the middle of the road, and the phrase is explained from its parts, the middle of the road being the part of it that leads where the traveler intends to go. What is said about the exchange is drawn out at length, since the verse connects the asking described before it with a loss that is described here as losing the way itself.

phrases.translation: Many among the People of the Book wish they could turn you ˹believers˺ back to disbelief because of their envy,
phrases.ar: وَدَّ كَثِيرٞ مِّنۡ أَهۡلِ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ لَوۡ يَرُدُّونَكُم مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ إِيمَٰنِكُمۡ كُفَّارًا حَسَدٗا مِّنۡ
phrases.explanation:
The verse is placed first. This saying of Allah makes clear that His address in all these verses runs to a particular group, and the discussion of that point is given at length, since it settles who is being spoken to and who is being spoken about.

The wish described is then explained. Many of the People of the Book wish that they could turn the believers back into unbelief, and the motive named with it is envy. The word for envy is explained, and the phrase from themselves is then explained as meaning from within themselves, as a person says in ordinary speech that something came from himself when it arose in his own heart.

A long discussion of the grammar accompanies these words, since the construction that carries the wish and the motive is one that Arabic uses in a particular way, and the explanation of it is set out in full.

phrases.translation: after the truth has been made clear to them.
phrases.ar: عِندِ أَنفُسِهِم مِّنۢ بَعۡدِ مَا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُمُ ٱلۡحَقُّۖ
phrases.explanation: The clause after the truth has been made clear to them is then explained, and its sense is that the truth had already become plain to the people described. The word is then drawn out for what it indicates, namely that the disbelief of those whose account Allah relates in this verse came after clarity and not before it, which is what makes the envy named in the verse a choice rather than a mistake.

phrases.translation: Pardon and bear with them until Allah delivers His decision.
phrases.ar: فَٱعۡفُواْ وَٱصۡفَحُواْ حَتَّىٰ يَأۡتِيَ ٱللَّهُ بِأَمۡرِهِۦٓۗ
phrases.explanation:
The command given to the believers is then explained. Pardon means overlook what proceeded from them of evil, and the explanation of the word is given at length, since it covers letting a thing pass rather than answering it. Turning away is joined to it, and the two together describe a conduct toward people who are actively wishing harm.

The limit set on that conduct is then noted, since the command runs only until Allah brings His command, so what is asked of the believers is patience for a period and not permanent silence.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything
phrases.ar: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيۡءٖ قَدِيرٞ
phrases.explanation: The closing name is explained by referring back to what was already demonstrated earlier, that the word for the all capable means the one who is able to do what He wills. It is mentioned here because the command before it asks the believers to wait, and the name tells them that the one they are waiting on is able to bring the matter to an end.

phrases.translation: Establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. Whatever good you send forth for yourselves, you will ˹certainly˺ find ˹its reward˺ with Allah. Surely Allah is All-Seeing of what you do
phrases.ar: وَأَقِيمُواْ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتُواْ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَۚ وَمَا تُقَدِّمُواْ لِأَنفُسِكُم مِّنۡ خَيۡرٖ تَجِدُوهُ عِندَ ٱللَّهِۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِمَا تَعۡمَلُونَ بَصِيرٞ
phrases.explanation:
The two commands are explained first. Establishing the prayer and giving the alms tax are the same two requirements named in the covenant described earlier in this chapter, and the statement concerning their explanation is given at length.

The promise attached to them is then explained. Whatever good you send forward for yourselves you will find it with Allah, and the sense given is that the good a person does is described as something sent ahead, so it arrives before him and is waiting for him rather than being lost when he leaves this world.

phrases.translation: The Jews and Christians each claim that none will enter Paradise except those of their own faith. These are their desires. Reply, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof if what you say is true.”
phrases.ar: وَقَالُواْ لَن يَدۡخُلَ ٱلۡجَنَّةَ إِلَّا مَن كَانَ هُودًا أَوۡ نَصَٰرَىٰۗ تِلۡكَ أَمَانِيُّهُمۡۗ قُلۡ هَاتُواْ بُرۡهَٰنَكُمۡ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
phrases.explanation:
What they said is explained first. The Jews and the Christians said that none will enter the Garden except whoever is a Jew or a Christian.

The wording of the claim is then examined. Concerning the word for Jews there are two views, the first of which takes it as a plural of a particular form and the second differently, and the grammatical discussion of both is given. It has also been said that the words except whoever is a Jew are in reality a statement of a condition.

The answer to it is then given in two parts. Those are their wishful fancies is described as a report from Allah about the standing of the claim, and the Prophet is then commanded to call on those who made it to produce their proof. Allah says to His Prophet to say to those who claim that the Garden is entered by none unless he belongs to one of the two groups that they should bring their evidence if they are truthful, so the claim is answered by a demand for proof rather than by a contrary claim.

phrases.translation: But no! Whoever submits themselves to Allah and does good
phrases.ar: بَلَىٰۚ مَنۡ أَسۡلَمَ وَجۡهَهُۥ لِلَّهِ
phrases.explanation:
The opening word is explained by referring back to what was set forth earlier, that the word translated as but no is an affirmation answering a negation.

The condition that replaces that claim is then explained. Whoever submits his face to Allah means whoever surrenders himself to obedience to Him, and the image is illustrated from ordinary speech, in which a person says that he has surrendered to obedience to the one to whose obedience even the rain clouds surrender. The report concerning the person Allah describes in these words is then given at length.

The second half of the condition is explained as well. While he is a doer of good means in the state of doing good, so the surrender is the direction of the person and the doing of good is what he is doing while he faces that way.

phrases.translation: will have their reward with their Lord.
phrases.ar: وَهُوَ مُحۡسِنٞ فَلَهُۥٓ أَجۡرُهُۥ عِندَ رَبِّهِۦ
phrases.explanation: The reward promised is then explained. His reward is with his Lord, and the statement concerning the explanation of these words is given, since the reward is described as being kept with Allah rather than as something handed over at once.

phrases.translation: And there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve
phrases.ar: وَلَا خَوۡفٌ عَلَيۡهِمۡ وَلَا هُمۡ يَحۡزَنُونَ
phrases.explanation: The two assurances that close the verse are then explained. No fear upon them is explained as concerning the Muslims who submitted their faces to Allah and did good, so the fear removed is the fear of what is ahead of them. They will not grieve removes what is behind them, and the two together are the same pair of assurances given earlier in this chapter to the people who believe and do righteous deeds.

phrases.translation: The Jews say, “The Christians have nothing to stand on” and the Christians say, “The Jews have nothing to stand on,” although both recite the Scriptures.
phrases.ar: وَقَالَتِ ٱلۡيَهُودُ لَيۡسَتِ ٱلنَّصَٰرَىٰ عَلَىٰ شَيۡءٖ وَقَالَتِ ٱلنَّصَٰرَىٰ لَيۡسَتِ ٱلۡيَهُودُ عَلَىٰ شَيۡءٖ وَهُمۡ يَتۡلُونَ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَۗ
phrases.explanation:
The verse is placed first. It is transmitted that it was revealed concerning a group of the people of the two religions, so the exchange reported here is tied to an actual meeting rather than to a general habit.

The explanation of the verse is then given. The Jews said that the Christians are not upon the truth, and the Christians said the same of the Jews, and each group said this while reciting a scripture of its own. That is the point the clause about reciting adds, since both groups have a book and both appeal to it, and yet each denies the other any standing at all.

A question is then raised about it. Did the Jews and the Christians have anything to stand on after Allah said this of them? The answer is given by referring back to a report transmitted earlier from Ibn Abbas, and the discussion that follows settles what the denial in the verse amounts to and what it leaves standing.

phrases.translation: And those ˹pagans˺ who have no knowledge say the same ˹about people of faith˺.
phrases.ar: كَذَٰلِكَ قَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ مِثۡلَ قَوۡلِهِمۡۚ
phrases.explanation:
The third group named is discussed first in its identity. The exegetes differed concerning whom Allah meant by those who have no knowledge. Some gave one answer, and others said that what is meant are the polytheists of the Arabs, because they were not People of the Book and so had no scripture to appeal to in what they said.

The correct view is then stated. Allah intended by His saying that those who have no knowledge speak in the same manner to the believers and to one another, so the likeness named in the verse is a likeness of speech, and a group with no book says about others what the two groups with books said about each other. The explanation of that is given at length.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah will judge between them on the Day of Judgment regarding their dispute
phrases.ar: فَٱللَّهُ يَحۡكُمُ بَيۡنَهُمۡ يَوۡمَ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِ فِيمَا كَانُواْ فِيهِ يَخۡتَلِفُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The judgment promised is then explained. Allah will pass judgment between them and so make a separation between the groups, and the verse names the day on which that happens.

The word for the Resurrection is explained from its form. It is a verbal noun from the saying of a person who says, I stood, with the forms given, and by it here is meant only the rising of the creatures from their graves before their Lord. The meaning of the Day of Resurrection is therefore the day of that rising, and the dispute named in the verse is what will be settled on it.

phrases.translation: Who does more wrong than those who prevent Allah’s Name from being mentioned in His places of worship and strive to destroy them?
phrases.ar: وَمَنۡ أَظۡلَمُ مِمَّن مَّنَعَ مَسَٰجِدَ ٱللَّهِ أَن يُذۡكَرَ فِيهَا ٱسۡمُهُۥ وَسَعَىٰ فِي خَرَابِهَآۚ
phrases.explanation:
The question is explained first by referring back to what was already demonstrated, that the meaning of wrongdoing in Arabic is putting a thing in a place other than the place it belongs to. The question who is more unjust is therefore not asking for a comparison among kinds of injustice but naming the worst placement of all.

The places named are then explained. The word used is the plural of the word for a place of worship, and it is explained as covering every place in which Allah is worshipped, so it is not limited to buildings of one kind or to one community. What was already shown about the word is referred to rather than repeated.

The clause about the mention of Allah's name is discussed next, and two manners of interpreting it are given. On one of them the preventing is described in terms of the places themselves, and on the other the meaning is, who is more unjust than he who prevents that the name of Allah be mentioned in them, so the thing prevented is the mention and the people prevented are those who would make it.

The second half of the description is explained last. Striving to ruin them means working toward their destruction, and the explanation given joins it to the preventing before it, since both are ways of ending the worship that those places exist for.

phrases.translation: Such people have no right to enter these places except with fear.
phrases.ar: أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ مَا كَانَ لَهُمۡ أَن يَدۡخُلُوهَآ إِلَّا خَآئِفِينَۚ
phrases.explanation:
The sentence that follows is explained as a report from Allah about the person who prevented the places of worship, so what comes next describes his standing rather than adding a new command.

The fear named in it is then discussed. It has been said that the wording is used in this particular form because of what the exception carries with it, and the explanation of that is given, since the verse does not forbid the people described from entering at all but says that it was not for them to enter except in fear.

phrases.translation: For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter
phrases.ar: لَهُمۡ فِي ٱلدُّنۡيَا خِزۡيٞ وَلَهُمۡ فِي ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٞ
phrases.explanation:
The two punishments are then explained. For them means for those about whom Allah reported what He reported in this verse, so the description runs back to the same people.

Disgrace in this world is named first and the tremendous punishment in the hereafter second, and the two are joined in one sentence so that what they receive is described in both worlds rather than in one.

phrases.translation: To Allah belong the east and the west,
phrases.ar: وَلِلَّهِ ٱلۡمَشۡرِقُ وَٱلۡمَغۡرِبُۚ
phrases.explanation:
The ownership stated at the head of the verse is explained first. By the words to Allah belong the east and the west, Allah means that both directions are His, so no direction is outside what He owns and none has a claim on Him of its own.

The word for the east is then explained. It is the place where the sun rises, that is, the place of its rising, and the same formation is used in ordinary speech for the place where a thing happens, so the word names a direction by naming what occurs in it.

A question is raised about the wording. Did Allah then have only one east and one west, so that it should be said that to Him belong the east and the west? The answer is given by noting that the two words are used in Arabic for directions in general and not for two single points, and the discussion of that point is set out.

The reason for singling out these two directions is then discussed. The interpreters differed concerning it, and several explanations are recorded one after another, with the reports naming who held each of them. What the answers share is that the east and the west are named because they cover the whole compass of turning, so a person facing any direction is facing something Allah owns.

phrases.translation: so wherever you turn you are facing ˹towards˺ Allah.
phrases.ar: فَأَيۡنَمَا تُوَلُّواْ فَثَمَّ وَجۡهُ ٱللَّهِۚ
phrases.explanation:
The word for turning is explained first. The most fitting interpretation of it is that it means you turn toward a direction, so the verb describes the facing of a person rather than the movement of his body from one place to another.

The word translated as there is then explained as carrying the sense of in that place, which fixes the second half of the sentence to the direction a person has turned toward.

The phrase there is the face of Allah is discussed last, and there is disagreement about it. Some said one thing, and others said that the meaning is that there is the direction Allah has appointed for prayer, so the face is read as the qibla. Others again said that the meaning is that by turning toward it a person obtains what Allah has attached to that turning. The reports naming who said each are given with them.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing
phrases.ar: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ وَٰسِعٌ عَلِيمٞ
phrases.explanation:
The two names that close the verse are then explained. The All Encompassing means that Allah encompasses all His creation, so nothing of it is outside what He holds, and the name is read together with the ownership of the east and the west stated at the head of the verse.

The All Knowing is joined to it, and the two together are what makes the permission given in the verse safe, since a person turning in any direction is turned toward something encompassed by Allah and known to Him.

phrases.translation: They say, “Allah has offspring.”
phrases.ar: وَقَالُواْ ٱتَّخَذَ ٱللَّهُ وَلَدٗاۗ سُبۡحَٰنَهُۥۖ
phrases.explanation:
The saying reported is explained first, and the explanation of the verse is then given in connection with what precedes it, since the claim that Allah has taken a son is answered by what the rest of the verse states about Him.

Allah then informs that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, in ownership and in lordship, and everything in them is under His command. That is the answer to the claim just reported, because what belongs to Him in that way, holding it and disposing of it, is not the kind of thing of which a child can be spoken.

phrases.translation: Glory be to Him! In fact, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth—all are subject to His Will
phrases.ar: بَل لَّهُۥ مَا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۖ كُلّٞ لَّهُۥ قَٰنِتُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The obedience stated at the end of the verse is discussed by the people of interpretation, who differed concerning its explanation. Some took it one way, and others said that the meaning is that all of them acknowledge servitude before Him, so what is described is a standing of everything in creation rather than the willing obedience of believers only.

The word used is then examined in the language. It has in Arabic several meanings, and they are listed, the first of them being obedience and the others following from it, including a standing long in prayer and a lowering of the self before the one obeyed.

The meaning most appropriate here is then chosen from among them, which is obedience, and the reasoning for that choice is given at length, since the sentence speaks of everything in the heavens and the earth and not only of people who worship.

phrases.translation: ˹He is˺ the Originator of the heavens and the earth!
phrases.ar: بَدِيعُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۖ وَإِذَا
phrases.explanation:
The name is explained first as meaning the originator of the heavens and the earth, so it names a bringing into being without a model already there.

A point of grammar is then given about the form of the word. In reality it is an active form that has been turned into the pattern used here, just as another word of the same kind was turned into its shortened shape, and the ordinary use of that second word is quoted, namely that a person brings about what he wills. A line of poetry is cited as a witness for the form.

The meaning of the verse as a whole is then stated. Glory be to Allah, and how could He have a child while He is the possessor of all that is in the heavens and the earth and the one who originated them. This is a notification from Allah to His servants, and it concerns the standing of those who bear witness to what the verse describes, since the origin of everything is what rules out the claim reported before it.

phrases.translation: When He decrees a matter, He simply tells it, “Be!” And it is
phrases.ar: قَضَىٰٓ أَمۡرٗا فَإِنَّمَا يَقُولُ لَهُۥ كُن فَيَكُونُ
phrases.explanation:
The decreeing named here is explained from its root. The basic meaning of every decreeing of a matter in Arabic is the determining of it and the completing of it, and the discussion of that meaning is given at length, since it fixes what kind of act the verse is describing.

The clause that follows is then explained in the same terms. When He determines a matter and completes it, He says to it, be, and it is, so the saying is attached to the determining rather than standing on its own.

A question is then raised about the wording. What is the meaning of saying that He speaks to a matter when a matter cannot hear speech? The answer begins by noting that the exegetes disputed concerning the meaning, and what they said is reported.

Some of them said that this is a notification from Allah concerning His irrevocable command, and that the description of it as speech is a way of stating that nothing stands between His willing a thing and its being, so no delay and no means come in between. The explanation of that reading is given in full.

The correct view concerning the saying is then stated at length. It settles how the words are to be taken, and the reasoning turns on the fact that the sentence describes the manner of Allah's acting rather than reporting a conversation, so the command named is the effect itself and not a sound addressed to something that listens.

phrases.translation: Those who have no knowledge say, “If only Allah would speak to us or a sign would come to us!”
phrases.ar: وَقَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ لَا يَعۡلَمُونَ لَوۡلَا يُكَلِّمُنَا ٱللَّهُ أَوۡ تَأۡتِينَآ ءَايَةٞۗ
phrases.explanation:
The demand is reported first, and then the people who made it are discussed. The exegetes differed concerning whom Allah meant by those who have no knowledge. Some named one group, with the reports of who said so given. Others said that what is meant are the Jews who lived in the time of the Messenger of Allah. Others again said that what is meant are the polytheists among the Arabs.

The three answers differ about the identity of the people and not about the thing said, since all of them agree that the demand was for Allah to speak to them directly or for a sign to come to them, and that the demand was made by people described as not knowing.

The description of them as having no knowledge is what the verse turns on, since the demand is presented not as a request for evidence but as the speech of people who do not know what has already been given to them.

phrases.translation: The same was said by those who came before. Their hearts are all alike.
phrases.ar: كَذَٰلِكَ قَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبۡلِهِم مِّثۡلَ قَوۡلِهِمۡۘ تَشَٰبَهَتۡ قُلُوبُهُمۡۗ
phrases.explanation:
The comparison drawn is discussed next. Thus also said those who were before them the like of their saying, and the exegetes differed concerning whom Allah meant by those who were before. Some named one group, and others said that they are the Jews and the Christians, on the ground that those who have no knowledge are the Arabs, so the two halves of the verse describe two different sets of people saying the same thing.

The reading preferred is then given, and it rests on what was already demonstrated earlier about who is meant by the first group, with the reasoning set out at length.

The likeness of their hearts is explained last. Another said that the meaning is that the hearts of the disbelieving Arabs and of the Jews and the Christians resemble one another, so what is being compared is not the wording of the demand but the state of the people making it, and the verse says that the hearts have come to look alike across groups that claim to be nothing like one another.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We have made the signs clear for people of sure faith
phrases.ar: قَدۡ بَيَّنَّا ٱلۡأٓيَٰتِ لِقَوۡمٖ يُوقِنُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The closing clause is explained as a statement that the signs have already been made clear, and that they were made clear for a people who have certainty.

The certainty named here is therefore what allows the signs already given to be seen as signs, and the demand for another sign is answered by pointing to what has been made clear rather than by promising something further.

phrases.translation: We have surely sent you with the truth ˹O Prophet˺
phrases.ar: إِنَّآ أَرۡسَلۡنَٰكَ بِٱلۡحَقِّ بَشِيرٗا وَنَذِيرٗاۖ
phrases.explanation:
The sending described is explained first. The meaning of Allah's saying that He sent the Prophet with the truth, as a bringer of good news and a warner, is set out at length, and the truth he was sent with is described as the message itself.

A question of recitation is then discussed. The reciters differ over one of the words in the verse, some reading it in the form that makes it a statement about the Prophet and others in the form that makes it a statement about what was sent. The correct view is the reading in the nominative, and the reasoning for preferring it is given.

Some of the grammarians of Basra are then reported on the second half of the verse, and their way of taking the clause that follows is explained.

phrases.translation: as a deliverer of good news and a warner. And you will not be accountable for the residents of the Hellfire
phrases.ar: وَلَا تُسۡـَٔلُ عَنۡ أَصۡحَٰبِ ٱلۡجَحِيمِ
phrases.explanation:
The clause about not being asked is discussed in the recitation. Most of the reciters read it with a vowel that makes it a statement, so the sense is that the Prophet will not be asked about the people of the blazing fire. Some of the people of Medina read it in the shortened form, which makes it a prohibition, so the sense is do not ask about them.

The difference between the two readings is then explained, since one of them reports what will not happen and the other forbids something, and the accounts of each are given with the reasoning behind them.

phrases.translation: Never will the Jews or Christians be pleased with you, until you follow their faith. Say, “Allah’s guidance is the only ˹true˺ guidance.” And if you were to follow their desires after ˹all˺ the knowledge that has come to you, there would be none to protect or help you against Allah
phrases.ar: وَلَن تَرۡضَىٰ عَنكَ ٱلۡيَهُودُ وَلَا ٱلنَّصَٰرَىٰ حَتَّىٰ تَتَّبِعَ مِلَّتَهُمۡۗ قُلۡ إِنَّ هُدَى ٱللَّهِ هُوَ ٱلۡهُدَىٰۗ وَلَئِنِ ٱتَّبَعۡتَ أَهۡوَآءَهُم بَعۡدَ ٱلَّذِي جَآءَكَ مِنَ ٱلۡعِلۡمِ مَا لَكَ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ مِن وَلِيّٖ وَلَا نَصِيرٍ
phrases.explanation:
The statement about their displeasure is explained first, and the explanation is given at length. The Jews and the Christians will not be pleased with the Prophet until he follows their religion, and what is described is not a displeasure that can be removed by meeting them part of the way.

The answer he is told to give is then explained. Allah said to His Prophet to say to these Christians and Jews that the guidance of Allah is the guidance. Allah commanded His Prophet only to call them to the guidance of Allah and to what He has declared.

The warning that follows is then explained. If you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, and the sense given is that this is addressed to the Prophet, the verse states what would follow, that he would have no protector and no helper against Allah. The knowledge named is what makes the supposed following a matter of choice rather than of confusion, and the absence of a protector is what makes the choice impossible to undo.

phrases.translation: Those We have given the Book follow it as it should be followed.
phrases.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ ءَاتَيۡنَٰهُمُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ يَتۡلُونَهُۥ حَقَّ تِلَاوَتِهِۦٓ
phrases.explanation:
The people described are discussed first. The exegetes differ over whom Allah meant by those to whom the book was given, and the answers are reported one after another with the chains naming who held each. Some said one group, and others said that what is meant are the scholars of the Children of Israel who believed in Allah and held His messengers to be truthful.

The reading preferred is then argued for. This saying is closer to the truth than the saying Qatada made, and the reason given looks back at the verses before it, which dealt with the same people, so the description here continues what the surrounding passage is about rather than introducing a new group.

The following named in the verse is then explained. Following the book as it should be followed is described in terms of what the book contains, and the explanation is given at length, since the verse makes the following and not the possession of the book the thing that counts.

phrases.translation: It is they who ˹truly˺ believe in it. As for those who reject it, it is they who are the losers
phrases.ar: أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ يُؤۡمِنُونَ بِهِۦۗ وَمَن يَكۡفُرۡ بِهِۦ فَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلۡخَٰسِرُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The pronoun is explained first. By the word them, Allah means these people of whom He reported that they recite the book as it should be recited, so the belief named here is attached to the group just described and not to readers of the book in general.

The connection between following and believing is then made explicit. Allah reported that the believer in the Torah is the one who follows what is in it, and He described those He described with the description of its followers in the same terms. What is reported about them is given at length.

The second half of the verse is then explained. Whoever disbelieves in it, and the sense given is that the disbelieving is in the book just named, is one of the losers, and the explanation of that is given, since the loss described belongs to the same act of following that the first half of the verse required.

phrases.translation: O Children of Israel! Remember My favours upon you and how I honoured you above the others
phrases.ar: يَٰبَنِيٓ إِسۡرَٰٓءِيلَ ٱذۡكُرُواْ نِعۡمَتِيَ ٱلَّتِيٓ أَنۡعَمۡتُ عَلَيۡكُمۡ وَأَنِّي فَضَّلۡتُكُمۡ عَلَى ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The address is explained first, and the meaning of the call to the Children of Israel to remember the favour Allah bestowed on them and to remember that He preferred them above the worlds is set out.

The favours themselves are not listed again here. They were mentioned previously, and the verse is referred back to that earlier listing rather than repeating it, so what is being asked of them is remembrance of what has already been set before them, and the preference named is the same preference described in those earlier verses.

phrases.translation: And guard yourselves against the Day when no soul will be of any help to another. No ransom will be taken, no intercession accepted, and no help will be given
phrases.ar: وَٱتَّقُواْ يَوۡمٗا لَّا تَجۡزِي نَفۡسٌ عَن نَّفۡسٖ شَيۡـٔٗا وَلَا يُقۡبَلُ مِنۡهَا عَدۡلٞ وَلَا تَنفَعُهَا شَفَٰعَةٞ وَلَا هُمۡ يُنصَرُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The warning is explained first. This verse is a warning and a deterrence from Allah directed to those who were addressed in what precedes it, and the explanation of that is given at length, since the verse names four things that will not be available on the day described.

The four are set out together. No soul will avail another soul anything, no ransom will be taken from it, no intercession will benefit it, and it will not be helped. Each rules out a way of escape that the people addressed relied on.

The exposition of all the meanings of this verse is then noted as having been given earlier, in connection with the corresponding verse that came before it, so what is added here is the fact of the repetition rather than a new reading of the words.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ when Abraham was tested by his Lord with ˹certain˺ commandments, which he fulfilled.
phrases.ar: وَإِذِ ٱبۡتَلَىٰٓ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمَ رَبُّهُۥ بِكَلِمَٰتٖ فَأَتَمَّهُنَّۖ قَالَ
phrases.explanation:
The testing named in the verse is explained first. By the word for trying, Allah means that He put Abraham to the test, and the verb is then set out in its Arabic form, with the shape of the past and present given and another use of the same word in the Quran cited as a witness for it.

The nature of the test is then explained. Allah's putting Abraham to the test was a trial by means of obligations that He imposed on him, so what is described is not a trial of patience in suffering but a trial of carrying out what was required.

The words with which he was tried are then discussed. The exegetes differed concerning their nature. Some of them said that they are the legal prescriptions of Islam, and that these are thirty portions. Others said that they are ten qualities from the established customs of Islam. The reports naming who said each are given with them.

The completing named at the end of the clause is explained last. By his fulfilling them, Allah means that Abraham completed the words, and the explanation of what that completing amounts to is given.

phrases.translation: Allah said, “I will certainly make you into a role model for the people.” Abraham asked, “What about my offspring?”
phrases.ar: إِنِّي جَاعِلُكَ لِلنَّاسِ إِمَامٗاۖ قَالَ وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِيۖ قَالَ
phrases.explanation:
The disagreement about the words continues, and the remaining answers are reported. Others said that what is meant is the statement I make you a leader for the people, so the words are read as the promise itself. Others said that they are exclusively the rites of the pilgrimage. Others said that they are matters of practice, among which is circumcision. Others again said that they are six things, and the six are listed as the star, the moon, the sun, the fire, the migration, and circumcision, each of them belonging to a part of Abraham's story told elsewhere in the Quran. The reports naming who held each answer are given one after another.

The correct view is then stated, and it is argued at length. It does not choose one of the lists as the exclusive answer but explains what the words named in the verse must be taken to cover, and the reasoning is set out in full, since the verse says only that Allah tried Abraham with words and that he completed them, without naming them.

An objection is then raised against that view. It is said that what Mujahid, Abu Salih and al Rabi ibn Anas said is more in agreement with the wording, and the objection is answered in turn, with the answer explaining why the particular lists they gave cannot carry the whole of what the verse states.

The promise of leadership is then explained on its own. By the words I make you a leader for the people, Allah said to Abraham that he would be followed, and the sense given is that leadership here is a being followed in religion rather than a holding of authority.

Abraham's question about his offspring is explained last. It is put in its place, after Allah raised his rank and honoured him and informed him of what He had made him, so the question is asked by someone who has just been given the promise and wants to know whether it passes on. The explanation of the question and of what it implies about his concern for those after him is given at length.

phrases.translation: Allah replied, “My covenant is not extended to the wrongdoers.”
phrases.ar: لَا يَنَالُ عَهۡدِي ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The answer to that question is explained first. This is an announcement from Allah that the wrongdoer will not be a leader followed by the people, so the answer does not refuse the promise outright but limits who it can reach, and the explanation of that announcement is given at length.

The covenant named in it is then discussed. The exegetes differed concerning the covenant that Allah withheld from wrongdoers. Some of them said that it is prophethood, and the meaning of the verse according to that view is that prophethood does not reach the people of wrongdoing.

A note is added about the reading of the sentence. In the reading of Ibn Masud the wrongdoers are made the ones who do not reach, so the sentence is turned around while carrying the same meaning, and the grammatical discussion of the two shapes is given.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when We made the Sacred House a centre and a sanctuary for the people
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ جَعَلۡنَا ٱلۡبَيۡتَ مَثَابَةٗ لِّلنَّاسِ وَأَمۡنٗا
phrases.explanation:
The verse is connected first to what precedes it. The statement that Allah made the House a place of resort for the people and a sanctuary is joined to the earlier verses by way of continuation, so the House is brought in as part of the same account rather than as a new subject.

The word for a place of resort is then examined. Some of the grammarians of Basra said that the extra letter at the end of the word was added on account of the great number of people who return to the place, so the form of the word carries the repeated character of the returning. The word is also given in its pattern, which is the pattern of a place noun, and it is derived from the saying of a person that the people returned to the place.

The meaning of the whole clause is then stated. By Allah's saying that He made the House a place of resort for the people, the sense is that He made it a place people come back to again and again, and the discussion of that meaning is given at length, with the reports naming who said what recorded with it.

The second description is then explained alongside the first. The House is made a place of safety as well as a place of return, and the two descriptions together say something about what the House is for, since people return to a place they are safe in and are safe in a place they keep returning to. The explanation given for the word therefore carries the repeated character of the returning rather than a single visit, and the security added to it in the second description is what allows that returning to continue, since a place people come back to year after year has to be a place where nothing reaches them.

phrases.translation: ˹saying˺, “˹You may˺ take the standing-place of Abraham as a site of prayer.”
phrases.ar: وَٱتَّخِذُواْ مِن مَّقَامِ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمَ مُصَلّٗىۖ
phrases.explanation:
The command about the standing place is discussed in the recitation. The reciters differ over the word. Some of them read it with the vowel that makes it a command, so the sense is take the standing place of Abraham as a place of prayer, and the reading is addressed to those who hear the verse.

Others read it differently. Some of the reciters of Medina and Syria read it with the vowel that makes it a report, so the sense is that they took the standing place of Abraham as a place of prayer. The two readings therefore differ about whether the sentence commands something or tells of something already done, and the accounts of each are given.

phrases.translation: And We entrusted Abraham and Ishmael to purify My House
phrases.ar: وَعَهِدۡنَآ إِلَىٰٓ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمَ وَإِسۡمَٰعِيلَ
phrases.explanation:
The charge given to the two of them is explained first. By the word for charging, Allah means commanding, so what follows is an instruction and not a report of what they decided.

The purifying named in the instruction is then explained, and the House is described as belonging to Allah, since the wording used is My House. What the purifying consists of is set out, and it is tied to the people for whose sake it is done, who are named in the rest of the verse as those who circle it, those who remain in devotion at it, and those who bow and prostrate.

phrases.translation: for those who circle it, who meditate in it, and who bow and prostrate themselves ˹in prayer˺
phrases.ar: أَن طَهِّرَا بَيۡتِيَ لِلطَّآئِفِينَ وَٱلۡعَٰكِفِينَ وَٱلرُّكَّعِ ٱلسُّجُودِ
phrases.explanation:
The three groups named at the end of the charge are then explained one after another. The first is those who perform the circumambulation, and the people of interpretation differ over the meaning of the word in this verse. Some took it in one way, and others said that those who perform the circumambulation are those who go around the House, whether they are residents of the city or people who have come to it. The reports naming who said each are given.

The more correct of the two interpretations is then chosen, which is the one given by Ata, and the reason is drawn from the word itself, since the one described by it is a person who goes around something. The discussion of the two readings is set out in full.

The second group is those who remain at the House, and here too the exegetes differ. Some of them said that what is meant is the person who sits in the sacred House without circumambulating and without praying, so the word covers a sitting that is not itself an act of worship of either kind. Others said that those who remain are the people who take up residence beside the House, so the word covers the neighbours of the sanctuary rather than visitors to it.

The third group is those who bow and prostrate, which names the prayer itself. The three together cover what is done at the House, and the charge to purify it is therefore given for the sake of everyone who comes to it in any of these ways, which is why the purifying is asked of both Abraham and Ishmael at once.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Abraham said, “My Lord, make this city ˹of Mecca˺ secure
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمُ رَبِّ ٱجۡعَلۡ هَٰذَا بَلَدًا ءَامِنٗا
phrases.explanation:
The request is explained first. By his saying, my Lord, make this a secure city, Abraham asks that the city be made safe, and the security asked for is then described as security from tyrants and from others gaining power over it, so what is asked is not merely an absence of fear but a standing that keeps others out.

A question is then raised about the request. If the sanctuary has always been secure, what was there for Abraham to ask for? The answer notes that there is a difference of opinion on the point, and some said that the sanctuary has always been protected in a particular way, which makes the request something other than a request for a new protection.

The correct judgment on this is then given at length. It explains what Allah did for the city and in what respect it became secure, and it distinguishes what was already the case from what the request added.

The outcome is described last. Mecca became what it is after Allah had protected it by repelling harm from it, and the discussion of that protection notes what was and was not imposed on its people in connection with it.

phrases.translation: and provide fruits to its people—those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day.” He answered, “As for those who disbelieve, I will let them enjoy themselves for a little while,
phrases.ar: وَٱرۡزُقۡ أَهۡلَهُۥ مِنَ ٱلثَّمَرَٰتِ مَنۡ ءَامَنَ مِنۡهُم بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلۡيَوۡمِ ٱلۡأٓخِرِۚ قَالَ وَمَن كَفَرَ فَأُمَتِّعُهُۥ قَلِيلٗا
phrases.explanation:
The second half of the request is then explained. Abraham asks that the people of the city be provided with fruits, and the request is limited in the wording of the verse to whoever of them believes in Allah and the last day.

The limiting of the provision to believers is what the rest of the verse turns on, since the answer that follows takes up the case of those who disbelieve separately. The explanation of the request and of the way it is worded is given with the discourse on the verse.

phrases.translation: then I will condemn them to the torment of the Fire.
phrases.ar: ثُمَّ أَضۡطَرُّهُۥٓ إِلَىٰ عَذَابِ ٱلنَّارِۖ
phrases.explanation:
The answer is discussed first in its wording. Others said that Abraham, the bosom friend of the Most Merciful, said this as a request of his to his Lord, so on that reading the words about letting the disbeliever enjoy himself are part of what Abraham asked for rather than part of what Allah said in reply. The report naming who said that is given.

The correct reading is then stated. According to us the correct reading and the correct interpretation are what Ubayy ibn Ka b said, and the reasoning is set out at length, since the two readings put the words in different mouths and therefore give the verse a different shape.

The letting enjoy is then explained. By him I will let enjoy for a short while, the meaning is that what Allah provides him with will last only a little while, so the enjoyment named is defined by its length.

The compelling that follows is then explained. By then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire, the sense is given, and the word for compelling is set out from its use in Arabic, since a person says I compelled someone to this matter when he constrains him to it against what he would choose. The meaning of the verse is therefore that he will be driven toward the punishment and made to reach it.

phrases.translation: What an evil destination!”
phrases.ar: وَبِئۡسَ ٱلۡمَصِيرُ
phrases.explanation:
The closing description is explained. By evil is the destination, the word used is discussed first, and it has already been shown that it comes from the word for misery, with the account of how the second letter of the form was changed given rather than repeated here.

The meaning of the statement is then given. Evil is the destination, and the destination named is the punishment of the Fire, which comes after the enjoyment of this world in which those described were living. The sentence therefore closes the verse by naming where the short enjoyment ends.

phrases.translation: And ˹remember˺ when Abraham raised the foundation of the House with Ishmael,
phrases.ar: وَإِذۡ يَرۡفَعُ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمُ ٱلۡقَوَاعِدَ مِنَ ٱلۡبَيۡتِ وَإِسۡمَٰعِيلُ
phrases.explanation:
The raising described is explained first. By Allah's words about Abraham raising the foundations of the House while Ishmael was with him, the sense given is that Abraham was in the act of raising them, and the verse places the two of them together at that work.

The word for the foundations is then explained. It is the plural of a singular form, and a single foundation of the House is called by that singular, so the plural names the parts on which the building stands. The grammatical discussion of the word and of its singular is given at length.

A disagreement about those foundations follows. The exegetes differed concerning whether Abraham and Ishmael raised the foundations of a house that was already there or laid them anew. A group said that they were the foundations of a house that Adam, the father of mankind, had built on Allah's command, so on that reading the two of them were rebuilding rather than beginning. The reports naming who said that are given.

phrases.translation: ˹both praying,˺ “Our Lord! Accept ˹this˺ from us.
phrases.ar: رَبَّنَا تَقَبَّلۡ مِنَّآۖ
phrases.explanation:
The supplication is explained first in its setting. By our Lord, accept from us, the sense is that Abraham said this while raising the foundations of the House, so the words come during the work rather than after it, and the explanation of that placement is given.

The question of who spoke them is then discussed. The verse according to one view has Abraham saying them, and the explanation of the verse on that view is set out. Others said that the one who said this was rather Ishmael, and the explanation of the verse according to that view is given in turn, since on this reading the supplication belongs to the younger of the two.

A further disagreement is recorded about the work itself. The exegetes differed concerning who raised the foundations, and this after they had agreed that Abraham was among those who did, so what is disputed is who else was involved and in what way. The reports of the various answers are given with the chains naming who held each.

phrases.translation: You are indeed the All-Hearing, All-Knowing
phrases.ar: إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ
phrases.explanation: The two names that close the supplication are then explained. By You are the All Hearing, the All Knowing, the sense given is that Allah hears the supplication the two of them have just made and knows what stands behind it, so the closing words answer the request for acceptance by naming the two attributes that acceptance depends on. The explanation of the words is given at length.

phrases.translation: Our Lord! Make us both ˹fully˺ submit to You
phrases.ar: رَبَّنَا وَٱجۡعَلۡنَا مُسۡلِمَيۡنِ لَكَ
phrases.explanation:
The next request is explained as continuing the same report. This too is a report from Allah concerning Abraham and Ishmael, that they both raised the foundations while asking, so the supplication in this verse is joined to the one before it.

A note is added on the wording of what follows. It has been mentioned that in the recitation of Ibn Masud the clause about the rites is read in a particular shape, and that reading is recorded because it bears on how the request later in the verse is understood.

phrases.translation: and from our descendants a nation that will submit to you.
phrases.ar: وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِنَآ أُمَّةٗ مُّسۡلِمَةٗ لَّكَ
phrases.explanation:
The request concerning their offspring is then explained. By the words and from our offspring a community submitting to You, the sense is that the two of them asked for a group from among their descendants who submit to Allah.

It has been said that by this they meant the Arabs, and the report naming who said so is given. That statement is then answered, since its contrary is indicated by the outward meaning of the Book.

The word for community is explained as well. In this place it means a group of people, and another use of the same word in the Quran is cited as a witness for that sense.

phrases.translation: Show us our rituals, and turn to us in grace. You are truly the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful
phrases.ar: وَأَرِنَا مَنَاسِكَنَا وَتُبۡ عَلَيۡنَآۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
phrases.explanation:
The request about the rites is discussed first in the recitation. The reciters differ over the word, and some recited it with a vowel that makes it a command addressed to Allah, show us our rites.

The proponents of that reading then differed among themselves over what the rites are. Some took them in one way, and others among those who read this recitation said that the rites are the places of slaughter, so on their reading the request is to be shown where the animals are to be slaughtered.

Others read the word differently again, with the vowel left out, and they claimed that its meaning is teach us, so on that reading the request concerns instruction rather than sight.

The verb itself is then explained. By the word for showing, the sense is direct me to it and make known to me its place, and it does not mean seeing with the eye, which is what settles the difference between the readings. The meaning is one and the same on either shape of the word, and the grammatical account of how the letters are dropped in one reading and kept in the other is given at length.

phrases.translation: Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations,
phrases.ar: رَبَّنَا وَٱبۡعَثۡ فِيهِمۡ رَسُولٗا مِّنۡهُمۡ يَتۡلُواْ عَلَيۡهِمۡ ءَايَٰتِكَ
phrases.explanation:
The request for a messenger is explained first, and a group of the people of interpretation concurred with what has been said concerning it, with the reports naming them given.

The reciting named in the request is then explained. By who recites to them Your signs, the sense is that he reads them out to those he is sent to, so the messenger's first work is described as carrying the signs to people rather than explaining them.

phrases.translation: teach them the Book and wisdom,
phrases.ar: وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ
phrases.explanation:
The book named is explained first. By the book, Allah means the Quran, and why the Quran is called a book was explained earlier, so the point is referred to rather than argued again.

The wisdom joined to it is then discussed. The people of interpretation differed concerning the meaning of the wisdom that Allah mentions here. Some of them said that it is knowledge of the religion and deep understanding in it, and the report naming who said that is given.

phrases.translation: and purify them. Indeed, You ˹alone˺ are the Almighty, All-Wise.”
phrases.ar: وَٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ وَيُزَكِّيهِمۡۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ
phrases.explanation:
The view preferred about the wisdom is then stated. The correct view of the statement, in our opinion, is that it is knowledge of the ordinances Allah has laid down, and the reasoning for that reading is given, since it explains why wisdom is named separately from the book even though both are taught by the same messenger.

The interpretation of the whole verse is then put together. Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from themselves who recites to them Your signs and teaches them the book and the wisdom and purifies them.

The purifying named last is explained from what was shown earlier, that its meaning is cleansing, and the discussion of what the messenger cleanses them from is given.

phrases.translation: And who would reject the faith of Abraham except a fool! We certainly chose him in this life,
phrases.ar: وَمَن يَرۡغَبُ عَن مِّلَّةِ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمَ إِلَّا مَن سَفِهَ نَفۡسَهُۥۚ
phrases.explanation:
The question at the head of the verse is explained first. Who turns away from the religion of Abraham, and the discourse on the interpretation of the saying is given at length, since the question is not asked for information but to rule the turning away out.

The exception that follows is then explained. Except him who makes a fool of himself, and the discourse on that saying is given in turn, since it names the only person of whom the turning away can be said.

A point of grammar is added about the form of the sentence. The word for himself stands in the accusative according to the meaning of specification, and the reason for that shape is explained, with the grammatical discussion given at length.

phrases.translation: and in the Hereafter he will surely be among the righteous
phrases.ar: وَلَقَدِ ٱصۡطَفَيۡنَٰهُ فِي ٱلدُّنۡيَاۖ وَإِنَّهُۥ فِي ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ لَمِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The choosing named first is then explained. We chose him in this world, and the discourse on the interpretation of that saying is given at length, including a grammatical account of the form of the word used for choosing and of what it carries.

The second half of the verse is explained as well. In the hereafter he is among the righteous, and the discourse on that is given in turn, so the verse joins what Allah did for Abraham in this world to the standing he has in the next, and the two are stated together as one description of him.

phrases.translation: When his Lord ordered him, “Submit ˹to My Will˺,” he responded, “I submit to the Lord of all worlds.”
phrases.ar: إِذۡ قَالَ لَهُۥ رَبُّهُۥٓ أَسۡلِمۡۖ قَالَ أَسۡلَمۡتُ لِرَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ
phrases.explanation:
The command is explained first. When his Lord said to him, submit, and the statement concerning the explanation of those words is given, including the grammar of the form used for the command.

The answer is then explained. He said, I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds, so the response names the one submitted to and covers everything other than Him, and the account of what that submission consists of is given with it.

phrases.translation: This was the advice of Abraham—as well as Jacob—to his children, ˹saying˺, “Indeed, Allah has chosen for you this faith; so do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission.”
phrases.ar: وَوَصَّىٰ بِهَآ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمُ بَنِيهِ وَيَعۡقُوبُ يَٰبَنِيَّ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ ٱصۡطَفَىٰ لَكُمُ ٱلدِّينَ فَلَا تَمُوتُنَّ إِلَّا وَأَنتُم مُّسۡلِمُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The enjoining named at the head of the verse is explained first. By his words that he enjoined this, the sense is that he enjoined this word upon those addressed, and by his words that Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, the sense is that he made it incumbent on them, so what is passed on is described as an obligation.

A point of grammar is then given about the wording. The word that would normally introduce the speech is omitted here, and the reason is that disclosing with the tongue is in meaning a form of speech, so the sentence treats it accordingly, and the discussion of that omission is set out.

The words enjoined are then explained. By Allah has chosen the religion for you, the sense given is set out at length, since the choosing is described as done for them.

A question is raised about the command that follows. Do death and life belong to the children of Adam in such a way that one of them could be forbidden to die except in a given state, and the question is answered, so the command is explained as concerning the state a person is to be in whenever death reaches him.

phrases.translation: Or did you witness when death came to Jacob? He asked his children, “Who will you worship after my passing?”
phrases.ar: أَمۡ كُنتُمۡ شُهَدَآءَ إِذۡ حَضَرَ يَعۡقُوبَ ٱلۡمَوۡتُ إِذۡ قَالَ لِبَنِيهِ مَا
phrases.explanation:
The question is explained first. The verse is put as a question to those who deny the messenger and hold to what came before him, asking whether they were present when death came to Jacob, and the answer given is that they were not, so a claim built on something they never witnessed is set aside.

The setting of the verses is then described. They came down as a refutation of the Jews and the Christians in what they claimed, and the people of interpretation spoke in accordance with that account.

The question Jacob put to his sons is then explained, and the sense of it is set out, so the scene the verse calls up is given before the reply is quoted.

phrases.translation: They replied, “We will ˹continue to˺ worship your God, the God of your forefathers—Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac—the One God.
phrases.ar: تَعۡبُدُونَ مِنۢ بَعۡدِيۖ قَالُواْ نَعۡبُدُ إِلَٰهَكَ وَإِلَٰهَ ءَابَآئِكَ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمَ وَإِسۡمَٰعِيلَ وَإِسۡحَٰقَ إِلَٰهٗا وَٰحِدٗا
phrases.explanation:
The recitation of the reply is then discussed. Some of the earlier reciters read the words as the God of your father Abraham, and the reading is explained.

The reading preferred is then given. The correct reading in our view is the God of your fathers, and the reason given is that it agrees with what the verse goes on to say, since the reply names Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac together and one father would not cover them.

phrases.translation: And to Him we ˹all˺ submit.”
phrases.ar: وَنَحۡنُ لَهُۥ مُسۡلِمُونَ
phrases.explanation:
The way the words are joined is then explained. The better of the two ways of reading them is that they work as a qualifying circumstance, so the submission named is what the reply itself adds to the worship named before it.

The order of the two names is then addressed. It has been said that Ishmael was placed before Isaac only because Ishmael was the elder, and the report of that is given.
